questions.promptText:
A company's IT help desk uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to turn each closed ticket into a knowledge article. The prompt template in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management describes the required layout: a title, a Problem part, a Fix part with numbered steps, and a Tags line. A wiki tool imports each article and rejects any other layout.
About 1 in 8 articles fails the import. These articles put the Tags line first or use bullets for the steps.
Which change will fix the layout with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add one complete article in the required layout to the prompt template as an example, and save the template as a new prompt version.
Add more detail to the layout description in the prompt template, and write the rules for the Tags line and the steps in capital letters.
Fine-tune the model on 600 past articles that passed the import, and change the application to call the new custom model.
Add an AWS Lambda function that checks each article against the layout and calls the model again until the article passes the check.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add one complete article in the required layout to the prompt template as an example, and save the template as a new prompt version.
This option shows the model a finished article. The model now sees the order of the four parts and the numbered steps, not only a description of them. Examples in the prompt show the model the output that the team expects. It helps the model match its output to what the team expects, and the outputs follow the style of the example. The change stays inside the prompt template, with no new code and no new model, and the application then uses the new prompt version.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.1: "Create effective model instruction frameworks to control FM behavior and outputs"
Example: "template configurations to format responses"

Sources:

  • Prompt engineering concepts
  • Provide examples (few-shot prompting)
  • Construct and store reusable prompts with Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Add more detail to the layout description in the prompt template, and write the rules for the Tags line and the steps in capital letters.
This option makes the same kind of instruction longer and louder. The template already describes the layout, and 1 in 8 articles still breaks it. Capital letters make the rules stand out, but they still do not show the model what a finished article looks like.

INCORRECT: Fine-tune the model on 600 past articles that passed the import, and change the application to call the new custom model.
A fine-tuned custom model can learn the layout from many past articles. However, the team must prepare the training data, run and pay for a training job, and move the application to the custom model. This is far more work than one change to the prompt template, so it does not have the least operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function that checks each article against the layout and calls the model again until the article passes the check.
A Lambda function that checks each article catches a bad layout, and a new model call can return a better article. However, the team must write and run this code, and each failed article costs extra model calls. The prompt stays the same, so the model keeps making the same mistake at the same rate.

questions.promptHtml:
A telecom company's support app has used an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents for two years. Customers sign in before they chat, so the app knows each customer's account ID and plan type. An AWS Lambda function in an action group needs both values to look up bills. Both values are required parameters of the functions, so the agent asks customers for them, and many customers type the account ID wrong.
The agent must not ask for these values. The function must receive the right values on every call, also in long sessions.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A telecom company's support app has used an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents for two years. Customers sign in before they chat, so the app knows each customer's account ID and plan type. An AWS Lambda function in an action group needs both values to look up bills. Both values are required parameters of the functions, so the agent asks customers for them, and many customers type the account ID wrong.
The agent must not ask for these values. The function must receive the right values on every call, also in long sessions.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Remove both values from the function parameters. Send them in sessionAttributes in the sessionState of the first InvokeAgent request of each session, and read them in the Lambda function from its input event.

Remove both values from the function parameters. Send them in promptSessionAttributes in the sessionState of the first InvokeAgent request of each session, and read them in the Lambda function from its input event.
Turn on memory for the agent with session summaries, so the agent keeps both values after a customer gives them once in an earlier session.
Remove both values from the function parameters. Save them in an Amazon DynamoDB table with the session ID as the key, and read the item in the Lambda function on each call.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Remove both values from the function parameters. Send them in sessionAttributes in the sessionState of the first InvokeAgent request of each session, and read them in the Lambda function from its input event.
Session attributes are values that the app sends to the agent, and they persist for the whole session. Every InvokeAgent request with the same session ID belongs to that session, as long as the idle session time limit has not passed. Amazon Bedrock sends the session attributes in the input event of the action group's Lambda function, so the function reads the right account ID and plan type on every call.

The agent asks the user only for the information that the function parameters need. When the two values are no longer parameters, the agent has nothing to ask. This is a built-in feature, so there is no new storage to run.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.2: "Build interactive AI systems to maintain context and improve user interactions with FMs"

Sources:

  • Control agent session context
  • Define function details for your agent's action groups in Amazon Bedrock
  • Retain conversational context across multiple sessions using memory

INCORRECT: Remove both values from the function parameters. Send them in promptSessionAttributes in the sessionState of the first InvokeAgent request of each session, and read them in the Lambda function from its input event.
Prompt session attributes also reach the Lambda function in its input event. However, they persist for a single turn, which is one InvokeAgent call. Values that the app sends only in the first request are gone in the next turn, so later calls in a long session do not receive the account ID and plan type.

INCORRECT: Turn on memory for the agent with session summaries, so the agent keeps both values after a customer gives them once in an earlier session.
Agent memory keeps summaries of past sessions, so the agent can recall earlier conversations with the same user. However, each customer must still give the values once, and the agent must not ask for them at all. The app already knows both values, so memory solves a different problem.

INCORRECT: Remove both values from the function parameters. Save them in an Amazon DynamoDB table with the session ID as the key, and read the item in the Lambda function on each call.
A DynamoDB table can store the values for each session, and the function can read them on each call. However, the team must create the table, write an item from the app for each session, and remove old items. Session attributes give the same result with no table to create or maintain, so this option has more operational overhead.

A travel company writes hotel descriptions with a model in Amazon Bedrock at a temperature of 0.8, for varied wording. Before each prompt release, an AWS Step Functions workflow sends 40 test inputs to the model, once each, and an AWS Lambda function checks each output for five required JSON fields.
The last prompt version passed all 40 tests. In production, about 1 in 25 outputs missed a field. When the team sent the failed inputs again, most of them passed.
The test must catch such a prompt before release, with the production settings.
Which change should the team make to the test?
questions.promptText:
A travel company writes hotel descriptions with a model in Amazon Bedrock at a temperature of 0.8, for varied wording. Before each prompt release, an AWS Step Functions workflow sends 40 test inputs to the model, once each, and an AWS Lambda function checks each output for five required JSON fields.
The last prompt version passed all 40 tests. In production, about 1 in 25 outputs missed a field. When the team sent the failed inputs again, most of them passed.
The test must catch such a prompt before release, with the production settings.
Which change should the team make to the test?

options.text: Send each test input to the model 5 times in the workflow, and accept the prompt version only when every output passes the check.
Set the temperature to 0 in the test workflow only, so the test outputs vary less from one run to the next.
Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the share of production outputs that miss a field, and roll back the prompt version when the alarm fires.
Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and review the test outputs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs after each test run.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Send each test input to the model 5 times in the workflow, and accept the prompt version only when every output passes the check.
The model samples each token from a probability distribution, and a temperature of 0.8 makes lower probability tokens more likely. So the same input can give a different output on each run. One run per input shows only one of these outputs, and that is how the prompt passed all 40 tests and still failed in production. Five runs per input, with every output required to pass, catch a prompt that fails only some of the time. The test keeps the production temperature, so it measures what users see.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.4: "Develop quality assurance systems to ensure prompt effectiveness and reliability for FMs"
Example: "Lambda functions to verify expected output"

Sources:

  • Influence response generation with inference parameters
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

INCORRECT: Set the temperature to 0 in the test workflow only, so the test outputs vary less from one run to the next.
A lower temperature makes the responses more deterministic, so the test would show less variation. However, production runs at 0.8, and the missing fields come from that variation. A test at another temperature can pass a prompt that still fails for users, and the test must use the production settings.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the share of production outputs that miss a field, and roll back the prompt version when the alarm fires.
An alarm on production outputs finds the problem and helps the team react fast. However, it fires only after users see bad outputs. The test must catch the prompt before release, so this is a safeguard in production and not a better test.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and review the test outputs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs after each test run.
Model invocation logging records the input and output of each model call in CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. The team could read every test output, but each input still runs only once. The logs show the same 40 outputs that already passed, so the test still misses a prompt that fails some of the time.

An energy supplier's mobile app answers customer questions about monthly bills. An AWS Lambda function sends each question, the meter readings and the tariff rates to an Amazon Nova model in Amazon Bedrock. The prompt tells the model to think step by step. In tests, answers were correct more often when the model wrote its calculations before the answer.
Customers now see a long list of calculations before each answer. Customers must see only the final answer, and the answers must stay as accurate as they are now. Each question must use one model call.
Which change should the team make?
questions.promptText:
An energy supplier's mobile app answers customer questions about monthly bills. An AWS Lambda function sends each question, the meter readings and the tariff rates to an Amazon Nova model in Amazon Bedrock. The prompt tells the model to think step by step. In tests, answers were correct more often when the model wrote its calculations before the answer.
Customers now see a long list of calculations before each answer. Customers must see only the final answer, and the answers must stay as accurate as they are now. Each question must use one model call.
Which change should the team make?

options.text: Ask the model to put its steps in a thinking tag and its answer in an output tag, and show customers only the text in the output tag.
Ask the model to write its steps first and then the line "FINAL ANSWER:" with the answer, and set "FINAL ANSWER:" as a stop sequence in the request.
Keep the instruction to think step by step, and add an instruction to write only the final answer, with no steps or calculations in the reply.
Send the reply of the model to a second model call that removes the steps, and return only the final answer from that call to the app.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Ask the model to put its steps in a thinking tag and its answer in an output tag, and show customers only the text in the output tag.
Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason before it answers. The Amazon Nova user guide shows a system prompt that puts the reasoning between <thinking> tags and the answer between <output> tags. The model still writes every calculation before the answer, as in the tests, so the accuracy gain stays. The app reads the text between the output tags and shows only that text to the customer. All of this happens in one model call.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.5: "Enhance FM performance to refine prompts iteratively and improve response quality beyond basic prompting techniques"
Example: "chain-of-thought instruction patterns"

Sources:

  • Give Amazon Nova time to think (chain-of-thought)
  • InferenceConfiguration

INCORRECT: Ask the model to write its steps first and then the line "FINAL ANSWER:" with the answer, and set "FINAL ANSWER:" as a stop sequence in the request.
A stop sequence is a sequence of characters that makes the model stop generating the response. Here, the model stops at the moment it writes "FINAL ANSWER:", so the reply contains the steps but no answer. The customer would see the calculations and nothing else.

INCORRECT: Keep the instruction to think step by step, and add an instruction to write only the final answer, with no steps or calculations in the reply.
If the model follows the new instruction, it writes no calculations before the answer, and the tests showed that answers are correct more often when the model writes its calculations first. If the model still writes the steps, customers still see the calculations.

INCORRECT: Send the reply of the model to a second model call that removes the steps, and return only the final answer from that call to the app.
A second call can remove the steps from the first reply. However, each question would then use two model calls, and the requirement allows one. The extra call also adds cost and time before the customer sees the answer.

Last week the team changed the reply style, and the extraction of dates broke. The team could not test the extraction apart from the other two tasks. The team wants to test and change each task on its own, with managed AWS services and no code to maintain.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company processes claim emails with one large prompt and a model in Amazon Bedrock. The prompt does three tasks in one call: it finds the claim type, extracts the policy number and dates, and writes a reply to the customer.
Last week the team changed the reply style, and the extraction of dates broke. The team could not test the extraction apart from the other two tasks. The team wants to test and change each task on its own, with managed AWS services and no code to maintain.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for each task, and connect the three prompts as prompt nodes in sequence in a flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows.
Keep the one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and save a new prompt version for each change so the team can compare the versions.
Write an AWS Lambda function for each task that calls the model with its own prompt, and run the three functions in order in an AWS Step Functions workflow.
Create an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents with one action group for each task, and let the agent decide which task to run for each email.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for each task, and connect the three prompts as prompt nodes in sequence in a flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows.
Each prompt now does one task. The team can test each prompt on its own in Prompt Management, with test values for its variables. In the flow, a prompt node uses a prompt from Prompt Management, its inputs fill the variables of the prompt, and its output is the response of the model. The output of one node connects to the input of the next node, so the three tasks run as a chain.

A change to the reply prompt no longer touches the extraction prompt, and a failed test points to one node. Prompt Management and Flows are managed features of Amazon Bedrock, so there is no code to maintain.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 1.6.6: "Design complex prompt systems to handle sophisticated tasks with FMs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows for sequential prompt chains"

Sources:

  • Node types for your flow
  • Construct and store reusable prompts with Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Keep the one prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and save a new prompt version for each change so the team can compare the versions.
Prompt versions keep a history of the prompt, and the team can go back to an older version. However, the one prompt still does all three tasks in one call. A change to the reply style can still break the extraction, and a failed test still does not show which task caused it.

INCORRECT: Write an AWS Lambda function for each task that calls the model with its own prompt, and run the three functions in order in an AWS Step Functions workflow.
This option splits the tasks, and each function can be tested on its own. However, the team must write, deploy and maintain the code of three Lambda functions. The team wants no code to maintain, and Amazon Bedrock Flows gives the same chain of prompts without it.

INCORRECT: Create an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents with one action group for each task, and let the agent decide which task to run for each email.
An agent chooses at run time which actions to take, so the three tasks do not always run in the same order for each email. The claim emails need the same three steps every time, and a fixed chain is easier to test. Each action group also needs a Lambda function or app code to run its action, which is code to maintain.

A company's IT team uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to plan weekend server updates. Each request lists about 40 servers, the order rules between them, and the hours when each server must stay online. The model supports extended thinking and prompt caching.
The plans arrive in a few seconds and are never cut off. However, about a third of the plans break an order rule. The team wants far fewer plans that break a rule. Planners can wait a few minutes for a plan, and the company must keep the same model.
Which feature should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A company's IT team uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to plan weekend server updates. Each request lists about 40 servers, the order rules between them, and the hours when each server must stay online. The model supports extended thinking and prompt caching.
The plans arrive in a few seconds and are never cut off. However, about a third of the plans break an order rule. The team wants far fewer plans that break a rule. Planners can wait a few minutes for a plan, and the company must keep the same model.
Which feature should the team use?

options.text: Turn on extended thinking in each request, so the model works through the rules step by step before it writes the plan.
Turn on prompt caching for the rules part of each request, so the model reads the rules from the cache.
Raise the maximum number of output tokens in each request, so the model has room to write longer plans.
Use intelligent prompt routing with a prompt router for the model family, so each request goes to the model with the best predicted response quality.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on extended thinking in each request, so the model works through the rules step by step before it writes the plan.
With extended thinking, the model breaks a large task into smaller steps and reasons through them before it gives the final answer. This chain of thought reasoning can improve accuracy, and it is most useful for multi-step analysis, such as a plan with many order rules. It adds latency and output tokens, but the planners can wait a few minutes. The team keeps the same model and changes only the request.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.2: "Create advanced problem-solving systems to give FMs the ability to break down and solve complex problems by following structured reasoning steps"

Sources:

  • Enhance model responses with model reasoning
  • Prompt caching for faster model inference
  • Understanding intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Turn on prompt caching for the rules part of each request, so the model reads the rules from the cache.
Prompt caching reduces the response latency and the input token cost when long parts of a prompt repeat across requests. It does not change how the model reasons about the rules. The plans already arrive in a few seconds, and the problem is the broken rules, not the speed or the cost.

INCORRECT: Raise the maximum number of output tokens in each request, so the model has room to write longer plans.
The output token limit sets how long a response can be. The plans are never cut off, so the limit does not stop the model from finishing. More room for output does not make the model check each order rule before it writes the plan.

INCORRECT: Use intelligent prompt routing with a prompt router for the model family, so each request goes to the model with the best predicted response quality.
Intelligent prompt routing sends each request to one of several models in the same model family, based on the predicted quality and cost. Some plans would then come from another model. The company must keep the same model, so routing breaks a requirement.

A hotel company's guest app has used an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents for a year. One action group has three functions, which an AWS Lambda function runs: look up a booking, change a booking, and cancel a booking.
Last week, a guest asked about the cancellation fee, and the agent cancelled the booking. Now the agent must ask the guest to confirm before it changes or cancels a booking. Lookups must run without a question.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A hotel company's guest app has used an agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents for a year. One action group has three functions, which an AWS Lambda function runs: look up a booking, change a booking, and cancel a booking.
Last week, a guest asked about the cancellation fee, and the agent cancelled the booking. Now the agent must ask the guest to confirm before it changes or cancels a booking. Lookups must run without a question.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Turn on user confirmation for the change and cancel functions, so the agent asks the guest to confirm or deny before it runs them.
Add a line to the agent instructions that tells the agent to always ask the guest to confirm before it changes or cancels a booking.
Configure the action group to return control to the app, and have the app ask the guest to confirm before it runs each change or cancel.
Add an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent with a denied topic for changes and cancellations, so the agent blocks these requests.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Turn on user confirmation for the change and cancel functions, so the agent asks the guest to confirm or deny before it runs them.
User confirmation is a setting for each action in an action group. When it is on, the agent answers with a confirmation question, and the guest chooses to confirm or deny the action. The function runs only after the guest confirms. The lookup function keeps confirmation off, so lookups run without a question. The app only shows the question to the guest and sends the answer back to the agent. The agent and the existing Lambda function still run the action, so the team adds very little code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.3: "Develop safeguarded AI workflows to ensure controlled FM behavior"

Sources:

  • Get user confirmation before invoking action group function
  • Return control to the agent developer by sending elicited information in an InvokeAgent response
  • Block denied topics to help remove harmful content

INCORRECT: Add a line to the agent instructions that tells the agent to always ask the guest to confirm before it changes or cancels a booking.
The agent reads its instructions, and most of the time it may follow this line. However, the model decides each time whether to follow an instruction, and last week the agent already acted on a simple question. User confirmation is part of the action itself, so the question comes every time the change or cancel function is about to run.

INCORRECT: Configure the action group to return control to the app, and have the app ask the guest to confirm before it runs each change or cancel.
With return of control, the agent sends the information that it collected to the app in the InvokeAgent response, instead of calling the Lambda function. The app must then ask the guest, run the function itself, and send the result back to the agent in another request. This works, but it is new app code for a check that the agent can already do, so it has more operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Add an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the agent with a denied topic for changes and cancellations, so the agent blocks these requests.
A denied topic makes the guardrail return a blocked message when a prompt or a response is about that topic. Guests could then no longer change or cancel a booking through the agent at all. The guests must still be able to do both after they confirm.

A model in Amazon Bedrock checks the photos, a second model checks the description for banned content, and a third model estimates a fair price range. No check uses the result of another check.
Sellers now wait about 45 seconds for a result, and the slowest check takes 18 seconds. Each check must keep its own model. The seller must receive one combined result, and the wait must be close to the time of the slowest check.
Which solution meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online car marketplace checks each new listing before it goes live. An AWS Step Functions workflow runs three checks one after another. A model in Amazon Bedrock checks the photos, a second model checks the description for banned content, and a third model estimates a fair price range. No check uses the result of another check.
Sellers now wait about 45 seconds for a result, and the slowest check takes 18 seconds. Each check must keep its own model. The seller must receive one combined result, and the wait must be close to the time of the slowest check.
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Put the three checks in the branches of a Parallel state, and add a state after it that combines the three outputs into one result for the seller.
Change the workflow from a Standard workflow to an Express workflow, and keep the three checks in the same order, each with the same model that it uses today.
Replace the three checks with one multimodal model in Amazon Bedrock that checks the photos, the text and the price in one request.
Start three separate workflows, one for each check, and have each workflow send its own result to the seller when it ends.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Put the three checks in the branches of a Parallel state, and add a state after it that combines the three outputs into one result for the seller.
A Parallel state runs its branches as concurrently as possible, and it waits until all branches end before it moves to the next state. Each branch calls its own model, so each check keeps its model. The output of the Parallel state is an array with one element for each branch, and the next state turns this array into one result for the seller. The checks no longer wait for each other, so the total time comes close to the 18 seconds of the slowest check.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.4: "Create sophisticated model coordination systems to optimize performance across multiple capabilities"
Example: "specialized FMs to perform complex tasks"

Sources:

  • Parallel workflow state
  • Choosing workflow type in Step Functions
  • Invoke and customize Amazon Bedrock models with Step Functions

INCORRECT: Change the workflow from a Standard workflow to an Express workflow, and keep the three checks in the same order, each with the same model that it uses today.
Express and Standard workflows differ in how long an execution can run and in how often a state can run. The workflow type does not make the states run at the same time. The three checks still run one after another, so the seller still waits about 45 seconds.

INCORRECT: Replace the three checks with one multimodal model in Amazon Bedrock that checks the photos, the text and the price in one request.
One request to one model can be faster than three requests in a row. However, each check must keep its own model, and this option replaces all three. The marketplace would also lose the specialized model for each check.

INCORRECT: Start three separate workflows, one for each check, and have each workflow send its own result to the seller when it ends.
The three checks now run at the same time, so this option looks close. However, the seller receives three separate results at three different times. The seller must receive one combined result, and no step here combines the three outputs.

A company's online store uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write product listings. An editor must approve each listing before it goes live. An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow sends each listing to the editor's review queue with a task token, and the review Task state waits for the callback.
When an editor is away, listings wait for days. If the editor does not answer within 4 hours, the listing must go to a backup editor. Every listing still needs an editor's approval.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's online store uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to write product listings. An editor must approve each listing before it goes live. An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow sends each listing to the editor's review queue with a task token, and the review Task state waits for the callback.
When an editor is away, listings wait for days. If the editor does not answer within 4 hours, the listing must go to a backup editor. Every listing still needs an editor's approval.
Which combination of steps meets these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Set TimeoutSeconds to 14400 on the review Task state that waits for the callback of the editor.
Add a Catch for the States.Timeout error to the review Task state, with a Next state that sends the listing to the backup editor with a new task token.
Set TimeoutSeconds to 14400 at the top level of the state machine, and catch the States.Timeout error there to send the listing to the backup editor.
Add a Retry for the States.Timeout error to the review Task state, with 3 attempts and a backoff rate of 2.
Change the review Task state to the Request Response pattern, so the workflow moves on right after it sends the listing to the queue.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set TimeoutSeconds to 14400 on the review Task state that waits for the callback of the editor.
A task that waits for a task token waits until the execution reaches the one year service quota, unless the state has a timeout. TimeoutSeconds sets the longest time that a task can run. When 14400 seconds (4 hours) pass with no callback, the Task state fails with the States.Timeout error. This step stops the endless wait and gives the workflow an error that it can act on.

CORRECT: Add a Catch for the States.Timeout error to the review Task state, with a Next state that sends the listing to the backup editor with a new task token.
A catcher on a Task state matches an error name and moves the workflow to the state named in its Next field. Here, the timeout from the first step moves the listing to a state that sends it to the backup editor and waits for that editor's callback. The listing still needs an approval, now from the backup editor.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.5: "Develop collaborative AI systems to enhance FM capabilities with human expertise"
Example: "Step Functions to orchestrate review and approval processes"

Sources:

  • Task workflow state
  • Handling errors in Step Functions workflows
  • Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions

INCORRECT: Set TimeoutSeconds to 14400 at the top level of the state machine, and catch the States.Timeout error there to send the listing to the backup editor.
A TimeoutSeconds value for the whole state machine also reports States.Timeout when the execution runs too long. However, catchers are available for Task, Parallel and Map states, not for failures of the top level execution. The execution would fail after 4 hours, and no state could send the listing to the backup editor.

INCORRECT: Add a Retry for the States.Timeout error to the review Task state, with 3 attempts and a backoff rate of 2.
A retrier runs the failed state again, so the listing goes back to the same review queue. If the first editor is away for days, the retries only make the listing wait longer. Nothing in this step sends the listing to the backup editor.

INCORRECT: Change the review Task state to the Request Response pattern, so the workflow moves on right after it sends the listing to the queue.
With the Request Response pattern, Step Functions moves to the next state as soon as it receives an HTTP response from the service. The workflow would no longer wait for the editor, so a listing could go live with no approval. Every listing still needs an editor's approval.

questions.promptHtml:
A company's returns agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Its refund tool calls an AWS Lambda function that sends a refund through the payment system.
Some customers received two refunds for one returned item. The logs show two tool calls with the same order ID, item ID and amount. Sometimes the model called the tool again after a slow reply. Sometimes the AWS SDK retried a call that timed out after the refund was sent.
A repeated call must never send a second refund. The agent must still receive the result of the first refund.
Which combination of steps will solve this problem?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's returns agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Its refund tool calls an AWS Lambda function that sends a refund through the payment system.
Some customers received two refunds for one returned item. The logs show two tool calls with the same order ID, item ID and amount. Sometimes the model called the tool again after a slow reply. Sometimes the AWS SDK retried a call that timed out after the refund was sent.
A repeated call must never send a second refund. The agent must still receive the result of the first refund.
Which combination of steps will solve this problem?
Select TWO.

options.text: In the Lambda function, build an idempotency key from a hash of the order ID, the item ID and the amount in the tool input.
In the Lambda function, create a new random UUID as the idempotency key each time the function receives a tool call.
Before each refund, write the key to an Amazon DynamoDB table with a conditional write. When the key already exists, return the stored result of the first refund and send no new refund.
Add an instruction to the system prompt of the agent that tells the model to call the refund tool only once for each returned item, even when a reply from the tool is slow.
Set the maximum attempts of the SDK client that calls the Lambda function to 1, so that the client never sends a call that timed out to the function a second time.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the Lambda function, build an idempotency key from a hash of the order ID, the item ID and the amount in the tool input.
An idempotency key names one operation. When the key comes from the inputs of the operation, every repeat of the same refund produces the same key. Here, the second call from the model and the retry from the SDK both have the same order ID, item ID and amount, so both produce the key of the first call. This is what lets the function see that the refund already happened.

CORRECT: Before each refund, write the key to an Amazon DynamoDB table with a conditional write. When the key already exists, return the stored result of the first refund and send no new refund.
A conditional write with attribute_not_exists succeeds only when no item with that key exists yet. The first call creates the record, sends the refund and stores the result. A repeated call finds the key, so the function returns the stored result and sends nothing. If the first call is still running, the repeated call finds the key with no result yet, so it sends no refund and tells the agent that the first refund is still in progress. Because the write is conditional, two calls that arrive at the same moment cannot both create a record. The agent receives the result of the first refund each time, which meets the second requirement.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.1.6: "Implement intelligent tool integrations to extend FM capabilities and to ensure reliable tool operations"

Sources:

  • AGENTREL06-BP04 Implement idempotent task execution patterns
  • DynamoDB condition expression CLI example
  • Best practices for working with AWS Lambda Event Functions

INCORRECT: In the Lambda function, create a new random UUID as the idempotency key each time the function receives a tool call.
A random UUID is a new value on every call. The second call for the same refund has a different key from the first call, so the function finds no record and sends the refund again. The key must stay the same for every repeat of the same operation, and a value that the function creates at call time never does.

INCORRECT: Add an instruction to the system prompt of the agent that tells the model to call the refund tool only once for each returned item, even when a reply from the tool is slow.
An instruction in the system prompt asks the model to act in a certain way, but the model does not always follow it. The instruction also does nothing for the second cause in the logs. The SDK retry comes from the client, not from the model, so the model never decides on it.

INCORRECT: Set the maximum attempts of the SDK client that calls the Lambda function to 1, so that the client never sends a call that timed out to the function a second time.
With one attempt, the SDK client no longer retries a call that timed out, so this removes one cause. The logs also show the model calling the tool again after a slow reply. Those calls still reach the function as new calls, and each one sends a second refund.

An insurance company hosts an open-weight LLM, which it never changed, on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The endpoint uses a large model inference (LMI) container, and the model writes first drafts of claim letters.
The model weights are in a 16-bit format. They fill about 70 percent of the GPU memory of an instance type with 8 GPUs, and this instance type often has no free capacity in the Region.
The company wants to run the same model on an available instance type with about half of that GPU memory. The claims team will accept the change if the letters still pass its review checklist.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An insurance company hosts an open-weight LLM, which it never changed, on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The endpoint uses a large model inference (LMI) container, and the model writes first drafts of claim letters.
The model weights are in a 16-bit format. They fill about 70 percent of the GPU memory of an instance type with 8 GPUs, and this instance type often has no free capacity in the Region.
The company wants to run the same model on an available instance type with about half of that GPU memory. The claims team will accept the change if the letters still pass its review checklist.
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Quantize the model weights to the FP8 format, and serve the quantized model with the LMI container on the smaller instance type.
Add speculative decoding with a small draft model, and serve both models with the LMI container on the smaller instance type.
Compile the model for the GPUs of the smaller instance type, and serve the compiled model with the LMI container on that instance type.
Keep the 16-bit weights, and set the tensor parallel degree to the number of GPUs on the smaller instance type, so that each GPU holds one part of the weights.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Quantize the model weights to the FP8 format, and serve the quantized model with the LMI container on the smaller instance type.
Quantization stores the weights and activations in a less precise data type. FP8 uses 8 bits for each value, where the current weights use 16 bits, so the weights need about half of the GPU memory.

In FP8, the weights fill about 35 percent of the GPU memory of the large instance type. The smaller instance type has about 50 percent, so the weights fit, with room left for requests. This lets the same model run on less expensive and more available GPUs, which is the goal here. A quantized model can be a little less accurate than the source model, so the claims team checks the letters against its review checklist before the switch. LMI containers support quantization as one of their optimization features.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.2: "Deploy FM solutions by addressing unique challenges of large language models (LLMs) that differ from traditional ML deployments"
Example: "by implementing container-based deployment patterns that are optimized for memory requirements, GPU utilization, and token processing capacity"

Sources:

  • Inference optimization for Amazon SageMaker AI models
  • The large model inference (LMI) container documentation

INCORRECT: Add speculative decoding with a small draft model, and serve both models with the LMI container on the smaller instance type.
Speculative decoding speeds up text generation. A small draft model proposes tokens, and the large model checks them. This improves latency, not memory. The large model keeps its 16-bit weights, and the draft model needs GPU memory of its own, so the models still do not fit on the smaller instance type.

INCORRECT: Compile the model for the GPUs of the smaller instance type, and serve the compiled model with the LMI container on that instance type.
Compilation optimizes a model for the best performance on one hardware type, without a loss in accuracy. It also shortens deployment and scaling time, because the weights need no compilation when a new instance starts. It does not change the 16-bit data type of the weights, so the weights still need more GPU memory than the smaller instance type has.

INCORRECT: Keep the 16-bit weights, and set the tensor parallel degree to the number of GPUs on the smaller instance type, so that each GPU holds one part of the weights.
Tensor parallelism splits the weights across several GPUs. Each GPU holds a smaller part, but the total memory that the weights need stays the same. The 16-bit weights fill about 70 percent of the GPU memory of the large instance type, and the smaller instance type has only about 50 percent of it, so the split weights still do not fit.

questions.promptHtml:
A travel booking company uses Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock to sort each customer email into one of 30 request types. The model also pulls the booking number out of each email. The app handles about 400,000 emails each day, and each result must return within a few seconds.
Nova Pro gives accurate results, but its cost is too high for this volume. In tests with a detailed prompt that included example emails for each type, Amazon Nova Micro sorted many emails into the wrong type. The company has a large set of past emails, but no checked results for them.
Which solution will lower the cost and keep the accuracy close to Nova Pro?
questions.promptText:
A travel booking company uses Amazon Nova Pro in Amazon Bedrock to sort each customer email into one of 30 request types. The model also pulls the booking number out of each email. The app handles about 400,000 emails each day, and each result must return within a few seconds.
Nova Pro gives accurate results, but its cost is too high for this volume. In tests with a detailed prompt that included example emails for each type, Amazon Nova Micro sorted many emails into the wrong type. The company has a large set of past emails, but no checked results for them.
Which solution will lower the cost and keep the accuracy close to Nova Pro?

options.text: Create a distillation job in Amazon Bedrock with Nova Pro as the teacher, Nova Micro as the student and the past emails as prompts. Use the distilled model for the task.
Fine-tune Nova Micro in Amazon Bedrock with the past emails as the training data, and use the fine-tuned model for the task.
Send the emails to Nova Pro in a batch inference job each hour, and store the results in Amazon S3 for the app to read.
Move the task to Nova Micro, and add a short description and two example emails for each of the 30 request types to the prompt, so that the model has more guidance.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a distillation job in Amazon Bedrock with Nova Pro as the teacher, Nova Micro as the student and the past emails as prompts. Use the distilled model for the task.
Model distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model, the teacher, to a smaller, faster and more cost-efficient model, the student, for one use case. The training data can be prompts alone. Amazon Bedrock sends the prompts to the teacher and uses its responses to fine-tune the student. This fits the facts: the company has past emails but no checked results, and Nova Pro already gives accurate results that become the training answers.

Nova Pro as teacher with Nova Micro as student is a supported pair. A narrow task with high volume is a good use for a smaller model that learned this one task.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.2.3: "Develop optimized FM deployment approaches to balance performance and resource requirements for GenAI workloads"

Sources:

  • Customize a model with distillation in Amazon Bedrock
  • Prerequisites for model distillation
  • Prepare data for fine-tuning your models

INCORRECT: Fine-tune Nova Micro in Amazon Bedrock with the past emails as the training data, and use the fine-tuned model for the task.
Fine-tuning trains a model on examples. For a task with one output for each input, each example needs a prompt and a completion with the expected output. The company has the emails but no checked results, so it has prompts without completions, and the job has nothing to learn the right request type from.

INCORRECT: Send the emails to Nova Pro in a batch inference job each hour, and store the results in Amazon S3 for the app to read.
Batch inference processes many prompts asynchronously and writes the output files to Amazon S3 after the job is complete. It suits large jobs that do not need an answer right away. The app needs each result within a few seconds, and an hourly job cannot give that.

INCORRECT: Move the task to Nova Micro, and add a short description and two example emails for each of the 30 request types to the prompt, so that the model has more guidance.
More guidance in the prompt can help a small model. Here, the team already tested Nova Micro with a detailed prompt, and it still sorted many emails into the wrong type. The longer prompt also adds input tokens to each of the 400,000 calls a day.

questions.promptHtml:
A food delivery company sends an event to a custom event bus in Amazon EventBridge each time a restaurant changes its menu. Several rules send these events to existing services.
The company plans to add new AI features one at a time, starting in 2 months. The first one will use a model in Amazon Bedrock to write short descriptions of new dishes. When a feature goes live, it must also process the menu events of the previous 30 days. Existing services must not receive any event twice. The team wants no backfill code to maintain.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A food delivery company sends an event to a custom event bus in Amazon EventBridge each time a restaurant changes its menu. Several rules send these events to existing services.
The company plans to add new AI features one at a time, starting in 2 months. The first one will use a model in Amazon Bedrock to write short descriptions of new dishes. When a feature goes live, it must also process the menu events of the previous 30 days. Existing services must not receive any event twice. The team wants no backfill code to maintain.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Create an archive for the menu events on the event bus now, and set its retention period to 35 days.
When a feature goes live, start a replay of the last 30 days from the archive, and choose only the rule of the new feature.
When a feature goes live, start a replay of the last 30 days from the archive, and choose all rules on the event bus.
Add a rule that sends each menu event to an Amazon SQS queue with the maximum retention period. Have each new feature read the queue when it goes live.
When a feature goes live, run a script that reads the last 30 days of menu changes from the company database and sends them to the event bus with the PutEvents API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an archive for the menu events on the event bus now, and set its retention period to 35 days.
An archive keeps the events that an event bus receives, so that they can be replayed later. An event pattern limits the archive to the menu events, and the retention period sets how many days EventBridge keeps them. With 35 days, the archive always holds the 30 days that a new feature needs. The team creates it now, so it already holds a full 30 days of menu events when the first feature goes live in 2 months.

CORRECT: When a feature goes live, start a replay of the last 30 days from the archive, and choose only the rule of the new feature.
A replay sends archived events from a chosen time frame back to the event bus that first received them. You can choose all rules or only specific rules. When the team chooses only the rule of the new feature, the feature processes the past 30 days of menu events, and the existing services receive nothing again. Replay is a built-in feature, so there is no backfill code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.2: "Develop integrated AI capabilities to enhance existing applications with GenAI functionality"
Example: "Amazon EventBridge to implement event-driven integrations"

Sources:

  • Archiving and replaying events in Amazon EventBridge
  • Creating replays of archived events in Amazon EventBridge
  • Basic Amazon SQS architecture

INCORRECT: When a feature goes live, start a replay of the last 30 days from the archive, and choose all rules on the event bus.
This replay sends the same 30 days of events to every rule on the bus. The new feature receives them, but each existing service also receives every event a second time, which the requirements do not allow.

INCORRECT: Add a rule that sends each menu event to an Amazon SQS queue with the maximum retention period. Have each new feature read the queue when it goes live.
The maximum message retention period of an Amazon SQS queue is 14 days. The features need the events of the previous 30 days, so the queue cannot keep them long enough.

INCORRECT: When a feature goes live, run a script that reads the last 30 days of menu changes from the company database and sends them to the event bus with the PutEvents API.
A script that sends past changes again is backfill code that the team must write and maintain. The new events also match every rule on the bus, so the existing services receive the menu changes a second time.

questions.promptHtml:
A logistics company hosts a dispatch agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Dispatchers will use the agent from a new single-page web app. They sign in to the web app through the company's identity provider, which supports OpenID Connect and issues access tokens.
The security team sets two rules. The web app must not hold or receive AWS credentials of any kind. The agent must reject every call that does not come from a signed-in dispatcher.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A logistics company hosts a dispatch agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Dispatchers will use the agent from a new single-page web app. They sign in to the web app through the company's identity provider, which supports OpenID Connect and issues access tokens.
The security team sets two rules. The web app must not hold or receive AWS credentials of any kind. The agent must reject every call that does not come from a signed-in dispatcher.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure a JWT authorizer for the agent runtime with the discovery URL of the identity provider and the client ID of the web app. Have the web app send each token as a bearer token.

Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to exchange each dispatcher's token for temporary AWS credentials, and sign each call in the web app with these temporary credentials.
Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Create an IAM user for the web app, store its access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and sign each call from the web app with these keys.

Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Run a service on AWS Fargate that checks each dispatcher's token with the identity provider and then calls the agent with the IAM role of the service for each dispatcher.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Configure a JWT authorizer for the agent runtime with the discovery URL of the identity provider and the client ID of the web app. Have the web app send each token as a bearer token.
AgentCore Runtime supports two kinds of inbound authorization: IAM SigV4 and JWT bearer tokens. For a JWT authorizer, you give the OpenID Connect discovery URL of the identity provider and the client IDs that the runtime allows. The runtime checks the token in each call, and it rejects a call with no valid token. The web app sends the dispatcher's token in the Authorization header, so it holds no AWS credentials. Nothing extra runs between the app and the agent.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.3: "Create secure access frameworks to ensure appropriate security controls"
Example: "by using identity federation between FM services and enterprise systems"

Sources:

  • Authenticate and authorize with Inbound Auth and Outbound Auth
  • Amazon Cognito identity pools

INCORRECT: Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to exchange each dispatcher's token for temporary AWS credentials, and sign each call in the web app with these temporary credentials.
An identity pool exchanges a token from an identity provider for temporary AWS credentials. Only signed-in dispatchers would receive these credentials, so the second rule is met. However, the web app would receive AWS credentials, and the first rule does not allow that.

INCORRECT: Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Create an IAM user for the web app, store its access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and sign each call from the web app with these keys.
The access keys of an IAM user are long-term AWS credentials, and the web app would hold them, which breaks the first rule. The keys also belong to the web app, not to a dispatcher, so the agent cannot tell whether a dispatcher signed in.

INCORRECT: Keep IAM authorization for the agent runtime. Run a service on AWS Fargate that checks each dispatcher's token with the identity provider and then calls the agent with the IAM role of the service for each dispatcher.
This design meets both rules. The browser holds no AWS credentials, and the service rejects calls with no valid token. However, the team must build, run and update a separate service that does the same token check that the JWT authorizer of the runtime does. That is more operational overhead.

It publishes a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric each time the model output fails the JSON check. The app calls the function through the alias live.
The team has a new function version with a new prompt. At first, only 10 percent of requests may reach it, for 10 minutes. If function errors or JSON check failures rise in that time, all traffic must go back to the old version, with no person acting.
Which combination of steps should the team take to release the new version?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's expense app sends each receipt photo to an AWS Lambda function. The function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock and returns the receipt fields as JSON. It publishes a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric each time the model output fails the JSON check. The app calls the function through the alias live.
The team has a new function version with a new prompt. At first, only 10 percent of requests may reach it, for 10 minutes. If function errors or JSON check failures rise in that time, all traffic must go back to the old version, with no person acting.
Which combination of steps should the team take to release the new version?
Select TWO.

options.text: Deploy the new version with AWS CodeDeploy and the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes deployment configuration.
Deploy the new version with AWS CodeDeploy and the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce deployment configuration.
Add CloudWatch alarms on the function errors and on the custom metric to the CodeDeploy deployment group, and turn on rollback when alarm thresholds are met.
Set weights on the live alias to send 10 percent of requests to the new version, and have an engineer watch a CloudWatch dashboard and change the weights.
Add an AWS CodeBuild step that sends 25 sample receipts to the new version before the release, and stop the release when any sample fails the JSON check.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Deploy the new version with AWS CodeDeploy and the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes deployment configuration.
On the Lambda compute platform, the CodeDeploy deployment configuration sets how traffic shifts to the new function version. LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10 percent of traffic first and the remaining 90 percent 10 minutes later, which matches the release plan. The shift works through a weighted alias, which can split traffic between two published versions of a function.

CORRECT: Add CloudWatch alarms on the function errors and on the custom metric to the CodeDeploy deployment group, and turn on rollback when alarm thresholds are met.
A deployment group can watch CloudWatch alarms. With rollback when alarm thresholds are met, CodeDeploy redeploys the last known good revision when an alarm is activated. One alarm on the function errors and one on the custom metric cover both signs of failure in the story, and no person needs to act.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.3.5: "Implement CI/CD pipelines and GenAI gateway architectures to implement secure and compliant consumption patterns in enterprise environments"

Sources:

  • Working with deployment configurations in CodeDeploy
  • Configure advanced options for a deployment group
  • Implement Lambda canary deployments using a weighted alias

INCORRECT: Deploy the new version with AWS CodeDeploy and the CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce deployment configuration.
LambdaAllAtOnce shifts all traffic to the new version at once. Every request reaches the new prompt from the start, so the plan of 10 percent for the first 10 minutes is not met.

INCORRECT: Set weights on the live alias to send 10 percent of requests to the new version, and have an engineer watch a CloudWatch dashboard and change the weights.
A weighted alias can send 10 percent of requests to a new version. In this design, though, an engineer watches the dashboard and changes the weights by hand. The requirement says that traffic must go back to the old version with no person acting.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS CodeBuild step that sends 25 sample receipts to the new version before the release, and stop the release when any sample fails the JSON check.
A test step with sample receipts can find clear failures before a release, and it is a good habit. It does not send 10 percent of real requests to the new version for 10 minutes, and it cannot move traffic back when failures rise after the release.
