A company's developers built an internal code review helper that calls the Chat Completions API through the OpenAI Python SDK. The helper calls an OpenAI GPT OSS model that the company hosts on its own Amazon EC2 GPU instances, behind an OpenAI-compatible server.
The company wants to stop running these GPU instances and use the same model in Amazon Bedrock. The helper reads its endpoint, its key and the model name from environment variables. The helper code must not change, and the team wants no new service to run.
Which combination of steps will move the helper to Amazon Bedrock?
Select TWO.

options.text: Set the endpoint variable to the OpenAI-compatible base URL of Amazon Bedrock Runtime in the company's Region, and set the model variable to the ID of the model in Amazon Bedrock.
Set the key variable to an Amazon Bedrock API key, which the OpenAI SDK sends as a bearer token.
Set the key variable to the access key ID of an IAM user that has permission to call models in Amazon Bedrock.
Rewrite the model calls of the helper with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) and the Converse API, and keep the same prompts.
Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that turns each OpenAI request into a Converse API call, and set the endpoint variable to the invoke URL of the API.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the endpoint variable to the OpenAI-compatible base URL of Amazon Bedrock Runtime in the company's Region, and set the model variable to the ID of the model in Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock offers the OpenAI Chat Completions API. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, the base URL for the OpenAI SDK ends in /openai/v1, and the SDK adds the rest of the path. GPT OSS models support Chat Completions on this endpoint. The helper keeps its code and only reads new values at start.

CORRECT: Set the key variable to an Amazon Bedrock API key, which the OpenAI SDK sends as a bearer token.
An Amazon Bedrock API key lets a client authenticate with a bearer token instead of AWS credentials. The bedrock-runtime endpoint accepts it for Chat Completions, so the OpenAI SDK can use it as its API key with no code change. For production, AWS recommends short-term keys, which take their permissions from the IAM principal that creates them.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.1: "Create flexible model interaction systems"

Sources:

  • Chat Completions API
  • API keys

INCORRECT: Set the key variable to the access key ID of an IAM user that has permission to call models in Amazon Bedrock.
An access key ID is part of AWS credentials, which sign requests with SigV4. It is not an Amazon Bedrock API key. The OpenAI SDK sends the value as a bearer token, so the request fails to authenticate.

INCORRECT: Rewrite the model calls of the helper with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) and the Converse API, and keep the same prompts.
The Converse API is a valid way to call models in Amazon Bedrock. However, a rewrite with Boto3 changes the helper code, and the requirements do not allow that.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that turns each OpenAI request into a Converse API call, and set the endpoint variable to the invoke URL of the API.
A translation layer in API Gateway and Lambda could accept the OpenAI requests. However, it is a new service that the team must build and run, and Amazon Bedrock already accepts the Chat Completions request format directly.

questions.promptHtml:
A car dealer group's sales staff write vehicle ads on an internal web page. The page calls an AWS Lambda function URL. The function runs on a Node.js managed runtime and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Each ad takes about 20 seconds, and staff see nothing until the whole ad is ready.
Staff must see the text appear while the model writes it. The company wants no API layer between the page and the function.
What should the company do?
questions.promptText:
A car dealer group's sales staff write vehicle ads on an internal web page. The page calls an AWS Lambda function URL. The function runs on a Node.js managed runtime and calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API. Each ad takes about 20 seconds, and staff see nothing until the whole ad is ready.
Staff must see the text appear while the model writes it. The company wants no API layer between the page and the function.
What should the company do?

options.text: Change the function to call the ConverseStream API, set the function URL invoke mode to RESPONSE_STREAM, and write each text chunk to the response stream as it arrives.
Change the function to call the ConverseStream API, keep the BUFFERED invoke mode of the function URL, and return the text when the stream from the model ends.
Create an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with the function as its integration, and have the function send each text chunk to the page through the connection.
Turn on provisioned concurrency for the function, so that each request starts in an execution environment that is already initialized.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change the function to call the ConverseStream API, set the function URL invoke mode to RESPONSE_STREAM, and write each text chunk to the response stream as it arrives.
A function URL has two invoke modes. With RESPONSE_STREAM, Lambda invokes the function with the InvokeWithResponseStream API, and the function can send results as they become available. ConverseStream returns the model output as a stream of events with small pieces of text. The function writes each piece to the response stream, so staff see the ad while the model writes it. Lambda supports response streaming on Node.js managed runtimes, which this function uses, and the page still calls the function URL directly.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.2: "Develop real-time AI interaction systems to provide immediate feedback from FM"
Example: "by using Amazon Bedrock streaming APIs for incremental response delivery"

Sources:

  • Invoking a response streaming enabled function using Lambda function URLs
  • Response streaming for Lambda Event Functions
  • Inference using Converse API

INCORRECT: Change the function to call the ConverseStream API, keep the BUFFERED invoke mode of the function URL, and return the text when the stream from the model ends.
BUFFERED is the default invoke mode. Lambda uses the Invoke API, and the result is available only when the payload is complete. The model streams its text to the function, but the page still receives the whole ad at the end.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with the function as its integration, and have the function send each text chunk to the page through the connection.
A WebSocket API can push each piece of text to the page as it arrives. However, it is an API layer between the page and the function, and the company does not want one.

INCORRECT: Turn on provisioned concurrency for the function, so that each request starts in an execution environment that is already initialized.
Provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments ready, which removes cold start delays. The 20 seconds come from the model writing the whole ad, and the function still returns the ad only at the end.

questions.promptHtml:
A law firm's document review tool runs as a Python service on Amazon EC2. For each case file, the service sends about 500 pages to one model in Amazon Bedrock from 40 threads. All threads share one boto3 client in the standard retry mode.
Within seconds, many calls return ThrottlingException. After about a minute, calls fail at once, with no retry. Case files arrive a few times each week. Every page must be processed, even if a file takes longer. All requests must use the same model in the current AWS Region.
Which change will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
questions.promptText:
A law firm's document review tool runs as a Python service on Amazon EC2. For each case file, the service sends about 500 pages to one model in Amazon Bedrock from 40 threads. All threads share one boto3 client in the standard retry mode.
Within seconds, many calls return ThrottlingException. After about a minute, calls fail at once, with no retry. Case files arrive a few times each week. Every page must be processed, even if a file takes longer. All requests must use the same model in the current AWS Region.
Which change will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Set the retry mode of the boto3 client to adaptive, so the client lowers its request rate when Amazon Bedrock returns throttling errors.
Keep the standard retry mode, and raise the maximum attempts of the boto3 client from 3 to 10, so each throttled call is retried more times.
Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, so Amazon Bedrock processes the requests in several AWS Regions.
Create Provisioned Throughput for the model with no commitment, and send all requests of the service to the Provisioned Throughput.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the retry mode of the boto3 client to adaptive, so the client lowers its request rate when Amazon Bedrock returns throttling errors.
Adaptive retry mode includes everything in standard mode and adds a client-side rate limiter. The rate limiter tracks throttling responses and changes the rate at which the SDK sends requests. It can delay a first attempt, not only a retry.

The rate limiter works per SDK client, so the 40 threads that share this client send at one shared rate. The AWS documentation names this case: a client that calls one resource at high volume and expects frequent throttling. The files take longer, which the firm accepts, and the setting adds no cost.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.3: "Create resilient FM systems to ensure reliable operations"
Example: "the AWS SDK for exponential backoff"

Sources:

  • Retry behavior
  • Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference
  • Increase model invocation capacity with Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Keep the standard retry mode, and raise the maximum attempts of the boto3 client from 3 to 10, so each throttled call is retried more times.
In standard mode, each retry takes tokens from a retry quota. The quota is scoped to one SDK client, so all 40 threads drain the same quota. When it is empty, the SDK returns the error with no retry, and that is what the calls show after about a minute. More attempts for each call use up the quota faster, and the threads still send at full rate.

INCORRECT: Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, so Amazon Bedrock processes the requests in several AWS Regions.
A cross-Region inference profile routes requests to compute in other AWS Regions. This can give the service more capacity, but Amazon Bedrock would process some requests outside the current Region, and the firm requires the current Region for all requests.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the model with no commitment, and send all requests of the service to the Provisioned Throughput.
Provisioned Throughput gives a model a fixed level of throughput, and AWS bills it for each hour until someone deletes it. Case files arrive only a few times each week. The firm would pay for capacity that is unused most of the time, or it would create and delete the Provisioned Throughput for each file. A free SDK setting meets the same requirements at a lower cost.

questions.promptHtml:
An accounting software company runs a help assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant sends each question to a configured prompt router. The router uses Amazon Nova Lite as the fallback model and Amazon Nova Pro as the other model, with a response quality difference of 5%.
A cost report shows that most questions now go to Nova Pro. In a test of 300 of these questions on both models, Nova Lite answered most as well as Nova Pro. Some short questions are hard, such as tax rule questions. The team wants fewer questions on Nova Pro, and Nova Pro must still answer the questions where it is clearly better.
Which change should the team make?
questions.promptText:
An accounting software company runs a help assistant on Amazon Bedrock. The assistant sends each question to a configured prompt router. The router uses Amazon Nova Lite as the fallback model and Amazon Nova Pro as the other model, with a response quality difference of 5%.
A cost report shows that most questions now go to Nova Pro. In a test of 300 of these questions on both models, Nova Lite answered most as well as Nova Pro. Some short questions are hard, such as tax rule questions. The team wants fewer questions on Nova Pro, and Nova Pro must still answer the questions where it is clearly better.
Which change should the team make?

options.text: Lower the response quality difference of the router from 5% to 1%, and keep Nova Lite as the fallback model.
Raise the response quality difference of the router from 5% to 20%, and keep Nova Lite as the fallback model.
Make Nova Pro the fallback model and Nova Lite the other model, and keep the response quality difference at 5%.
Add code before the router that sends each question shorter than 15 words straight to Nova Lite, and send the other questions to the router.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Raise the response quality difference of the router from 5% to 20%, and keep Nova Lite as the fallback model.
The response quality difference decides when the router leaves the fallback model, which here is Nova Lite. With 20%, the router sends a question to Nova Pro only when it predicts that the answer of Nova Pro is more than 20% better than the answer of Nova Lite. Questions where both models answer equally well stay on Nova Lite, which lowers the cost.

The router predicts the quality for each question, so a question where Nova Pro is clearly better still goes to Nova Pro, whether the question is short or long.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.4.4: "Develop intelligent model routing systems to optimize model selection"
Example: "intelligent model routing based on metrics"

Sources:

  • Understanding intelligent prompt routing in Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Lower the response quality difference of the router from 5% to 1%, and keep Nova Lite as the fallback model.
A lower response quality difference makes the router switch more easily. With 1%, a question goes to Nova Pro when the predicted quality of Nova Pro is only slightly higher than the quality of Nova Lite. Even more questions go to Nova Pro, and the cost rises.

INCORRECT: Make Nova Pro the fallback model and Nova Lite the other model, and keep the response quality difference at 5%.
The fallback model is the starting point of the router. With Nova Pro as the fallback model, a question goes to Nova Lite only when Nova Lite is predicted to be more than 5% better than Nova Pro. The many questions where both models answer equally well stay on Nova Pro, so the cost does not go down.

INCORRECT: Add code before the router that sends each question shorter than 15 words straight to Nova Lite, and send the other questions to the router.
This rule looks at the length of a question and not at the quality of the answers. The team found that some short questions are hard, such as tax rule questions. These questions would go to Nova Lite, even when Nova Pro gives a clearly better answer. The team would also need to build and maintain the extra code.

questions.promptHtml:
A tax advisory company has a mobile app that creates a yearly summary of a client's receipts. The app calls an edge-optimized REST API in Amazon API Gateway. Behind the API, an AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock and returns the summary in the response.
Each summary takes 2 to 6 minutes to generate, and most requests end with a timeout error. Clients often close the app while they wait. The summary must be ready for them when they open the app again.
Which combination of steps should the team take?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A tax advisory company has a mobile app that creates a yearly summary of a client's receipts. The app calls an edge-optimized REST API in Amazon API Gateway. Behind the API, an AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock and returns the summary in the response.
Each summary takes 2 to 6 minutes to generate, and most requests end with a timeout error. Clients often close the app while they wait. The summary must be ready for them when they open the app again.
Which combination of steps should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Ask AWS for a quota increase that raises the integration timeout of the API to 10 minutes, and raise the timeout of the Lambda function to 10 minutes too.
Change the Lambda function behind the API to send each request to an Amazon SQS queue with a new job ID, and to return the job ID to the app at once.
Set the response transfer mode of the API method to STREAM, and change the Lambda function to stream each part of the summary to the app while the model is still writing the summary.
Add a second Lambda function that reads the queue, calls the model and stores each summary with its job ID, and add an API method that returns the summary for a job ID.
Change the app to retry each request that ends with a timeout error, with exponential backoff, until the API returns a summary.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change the Lambda function behind the API to send each request to an Amazon SQS queue with a new job ID, and to return the job ID to the app at once.
With this step, the API answers within a few seconds, long before the timeout. The app keeps the job ID, so it can ask for the result later, also after the client closes the app and opens it again. The queue keeps each request until a worker processes it.

CORRECT: Add a second Lambda function that reads the queue, calls the model and stores each summary with its job ID, and add an API method that returns the summary for a job ID.
Lambda polls the queue and runs this function with batches of messages, so the long model call runs outside the API request. The function stores each summary under its job ID, for example in Amazon DynamoDB. When the client opens the app again, the app calls the new method with the job ID and shows the summary.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.1: "Create FM API interfaces to address the specific requirements of GenAI workloads"

Sources:

  • Quotas for configuring and running a REST API in API Gateway
  • Stream the integration response for your proxy integrations in API Gateway
  • Using Lambda with Amazon SQS

INCORRECT: Ask AWS for a quota increase that raises the integration timeout of the API to 10 minutes, and raise the timeout of the Lambda function to 10 minutes too.
For an edge-optimized API, the integration timeout is at most 29 seconds, and this quota cannot be raised. Only Regional and private APIs can raise the integration timeout above 29 seconds. A longer wait would also not help the clients who close the app.

INCORRECT: Set the response transfer mode of the API method to STREAM, and change the Lambda function to stream each part of the summary to the app while the model is still writing the summary.
A REST API can stream the response of a Lambda proxy integration for up to 15 minutes. The stream reaches the app only while the connection is open. When a client closes the app, the connection ends, and the app cannot read the summary later.

INCORRECT: Change the app to retry each request that ends with a timeout error, with exponential backoff, until the API returns a summary.
Each retry starts the same long generation again, and each one ends at the same 29-second limit. Retries with backoff help with short, temporary errors. They do not help with work that always takes longer than the timeout.

questions.promptHtml:
A grocery chain has 14 regional managers who use Amazon Quick every day. Their sales dashboards are in Quick, and the weekly price changes are in a Quick space. Each Monday, every manager reads both and writes a short note for the stores.
The managers want to automate this short task themselves, with no code. Each manager wants to describe the steps in plain words and let the tool build the workflow. Each manager will own, change and run a personal workflow, and share good ones with the others.
Which solution is the MOST suitable for these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A grocery chain has 14 regional managers who use Amazon Quick every day. Their sales dashboards are in Quick, and the weekly price changes are in a Quick space. Each Monday, every manager reads both and writes a short note for the stores.
The managers want to automate this short task themselves, with no code. Each manager wants to describe the steps in plain words and let the tool build the workflow. Each manager will own, change and run a personal workflow, and share good ones with the others.
Which solution is the MOST suitable for these requirements?

options.text: Have each manager describe the process in Amazon Quick Automate, which creates an automation from the description. Each manager then edits and runs the automation and publishes it for the other managers.
Have each manager build a flow app in Amazon Bedrock in SageMaker Unified Studio, and drag prompt and knowledge base nodes onto the flow builder and connect them.
Have each manager describe the task in Amazon Quick Flows, which generates a flow from the description. Each manager then edits and runs the flow and shares it with the other managers.
Ask the IT team to write an AWS Lambda function that reads the sales data and the price documents, calls a model in Amazon Bedrock, and emails each note to the stores.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Have each manager describe the task in Amazon Quick Flows, which generates a flow from the description. Each manager then edits and runs the flow and shares it with the other managers.
Amazon Quick Flows lets any user create, change and share workflows that automate routine tasks, with no technical skills. A manager can describe the task in natural language, and Quick Flows generates the flow from that description.

The flow can use a dashboards step for the sales dashboards and a Quick data step for the price changes in the space. Each manager can then edit the flow, run it when needed, and share it with other Quick users. AWS describes Quick Flows for personal and team tasks that individual users run, such as drafting content, and this weekly note is that kind of task.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.2: "Develop accessible AI interfaces to accelerate adoption and integration of FMs"

Sources:

  • Using Amazon Quick Flows
  • Using Amazon Quick automations
  • Build a flow app with Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Have each manager describe the process in Amazon Quick Automate, which creates an automation from the description. Each manager then edits and runs the automation and publishes it for the other managers.
Like Quick Flows, Amazon Quick Automate creates automations from a description in natural language, so this option sounds close to the right one. However, AWS describes Quick Automate for centralized, enterprise-wide automations, especially those that run independent of one user, and for long-running and high-volume processes such as invoice processing. Here, each manager owns a personal workflow for a short weekly note and runs it alone. For personal and team tasks that individual users run, AWS points to Quick Flows.

INCORRECT: Have each manager build a flow app in Amazon Bedrock in SageMaker Unified Studio, and drag prompt and knowledge base nodes onto the flow builder and connect them.
A flow app links prompts, models and other units of work, such as a knowledge base, into a workflow, and the managers would build it in a visual interface, not in code. However, in the flow builder, a person drags each node onto the page and connects the nodes by hand. The managers want to describe the steps in plain words and let the tool build the workflow from that description, so this option does not meet the requirements.

INCORRECT: Ask the IT team to write an AWS Lambda function that reads the sales data and the price documents, calls a model in Amazon Bedrock, and emails each note to the stores.
An AWS Lambda function runs code that the IT team must write and maintain. The function could produce the notes, but the managers want to automate the task themselves, with no code. The managers also could not change the steps without help from the IT team.

A logistics company keeps about 60,000 scanned delivery forms as PDF files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Once a month, an AWS Lambda function lists the files. For each file, the function calls Amazon Textract and then a model in Amazon Bedrock, which writes a short delivery record. Each file takes about 10 seconds. The function stops at its 15-minute timeout after about 90 files.
The team wants up to 100 files processed at the same time, within the account's Amazon Bedrock quota. The team must manage no servers.
How should the team process the files?
questions.promptText:
A logistics company keeps about 60,000 scanned delivery forms as PDF files in an Amazon S3 bucket. Once a month, an AWS Lambda function lists the files. For each file, the function calls Amazon Textract and then a model in Amazon Bedrock, which writes a short delivery record. Each file takes about 10 seconds. The function stops at its 15-minute timeout after about 90 files.
The team wants up to 100 files processed at the same time, within the account's Amazon Bedrock quota. The team must manage no servers.
How should the team process the files?

options.text: Create an AWS Step Functions workflow with a Map state in Inline mode that takes the list of objects from a previous step, runs the steps for each file and sets the maximum concurrency to 100.
Raise the memory of the Lambda function to the maximum, so that the function runs each step faster and finishes the whole loop within its timeout.
Run the same loop on an Amazon EC2 instance with 100 threads, and stop the instance when the last file is done.
Create an AWS Step Functions workflow with a Map state in Distributed mode that reads the objects in the bucket, runs a child workflow for each file and sets the maximum concurrency to 100.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an AWS Step Functions workflow with a Map state in Distributed mode that reads the objects in the bucket, runs a child workflow for each file and sets the maximum concurrency to 100.
A Map state in Distributed mode runs each item in its own child workflow execution, and each child workflow has its own execution history. It can use a large set of Amazon S3 objects as its dataset, and the team can set how many child workflows run at the same time. A limit of 100 keeps the calls within the Amazon Bedrock quota, and Step Functions runs the workflow with no servers to manage.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.3: "Create business system enhancements"
Example: "Step Functions to orchestrate document processing systems"

Sources:

  • Using Map state in Distributed mode for large-scale parallel workloads in Step Functions
  • Using Map state in Inline mode in Step Functions workflows
  • Lambda quotas

INCORRECT: Create an AWS Step Functions workflow with a Map state in Inline mode that takes the list of objects from a previous step, runs the steps for each file and sets the maximum concurrency to 100.
In Inline mode, a Map state runs at most 40 iterations at the same time, so the team cannot reach 100. All iterations also add to the history of one execution, and Inline mode fits only when that history stays under 25,000 entries. Several steps for each of 60,000 files go far past that limit.

INCORRECT: Raise the memory of the Lambda function to the maximum, so that the function runs each step faster and finishes the whole loop within its timeout.
A Lambda function can run for at most 15 minutes. At about 10 seconds for each file, 60,000 files need about 7 days of work in one loop. More memory gives the function more CPU power, but even a much faster loop cannot fit that work into 15 minutes.

INCORRECT: Run the same loop on an Amazon EC2 instance with 100 threads, and stop the instance when the last file is done.
An EC2 instance with 100 threads can process the files in parallel. The team must then run and maintain a server, and the team must manage no servers.

The README in the code repository still describes the setup steps of an older version, because nobody updates the README after code changes. The README also has a support contact section and a license section that the team wrote by hand. These two sections must stay as they are.
The developers use Amazon Q Developer in their IDE. The team wants the README to match the code with no manual writing, and the team wants to review each change before the README changes.
What should a developer do?

options.text: In the IDE, ask Amazon Q Developer in the chat to create a new README for the project folder, review the diff and choose Accept.
In the IDE, ask Amazon Q Developer in the chat to update the README with the recent code changes, review the diff and choose Accept.
Turn on inline code suggestions in the IDE, and write the new setup steps into the README with help from the suggestions.
Create a Lambda function that sends the whole code base to a model in Amazon Bedrock each night and saves the reply as the README.

In the chat, Amazon Q Developer can update an existing README with recent code changes. It shows a diff of the changes, and the developer reviews the diff and chooses Accept to update the README in place. Amazon Q updates the existing README, and the developer checks each change in the diff, so the sections that the team wrote by hand stay. Nobody writes the setup steps by hand.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.4: "Enhance developer productivity to accelerate development workflows for GenAI applications"

Sources:

  • Generating and updating READMEs with Amazon Q Developer
  • Generating documentation with Amazon Q Developer

INCORRECT: In the IDE, ask Amazon Q Developer in the chat to create a new README for the project folder, review the diff and choose Accept.
When a README already exists and the developer asks for a new README, Amazon Q Developer overwrites the existing README instead of updating it. The support contact section and the license section, which the team wrote by hand, would be lost.

INCORRECT: Turn on inline code suggestions in the IDE, and write the new setup steps into the README with help from the suggestions.
With this option, a developer still writes the new setup steps by hand, even with help from the suggestions. The team wants the README to match the code with no manual writing.

INCORRECT: Create a Lambda function that sends the whole code base to a model in Amazon Bedrock each night and saves the reply as the README.
This function replaces the whole README each night, and nobody reviews the change before the function saves it. The sections that the team wrote by hand would not stay as they are. The team would also need to build and maintain the function.

Many customer messages need two or three specialists, for example: "My washer broke. Is it still under warranty, and when will the new part arrive?" Other messages need only one. Each message must use only the specialists that it needs, and each customer must receive one reply.
Which design meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A home appliance company builds a support assistant with Strands Agents. The assistant has three specialist agents for warranties, orders and repairs, and each one has its own instructions and tools. In a test, a single agent with all the tools and all the instructions often chose the wrong tool.
Many customer messages need two or three specialists, for example: "My washer broke. Is it still under warranty, and when will the new part arrive?" Other messages need only one. Each message must use only the specialists that it needs, and each customer must receive one reply.
Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a model to classify each message, send the message to the one specialist agent that fits best, and send the reply of that agent to the customer.
Create a graph that runs the warranty agent, the order agent and the repair agent in a fixed order for every message, and send the output of the last agent as the reply.
Create an orchestrator agent that has each specialist agent as a tool, and let the orchestrator combine the results of the specialists that it calls into one reply.
Create one agent that has the tools of all three specialists, and put the instructions of all three specialists in its system prompt.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an orchestrator agent that has each specialist agent as a tool, and let the orchestrator combine the results of the specialists that it calls into one reply.
In the agents-as-tools pattern, each specialist agent becomes a tool that another agent can call. The orchestrator decides which specialists to consult for each message, so a simple warranty question calls only the warranty agent, and the washer message calls the warranty agent and the order agent. The orchestrator then combines the input from the specialists into the reply to the customer. Each specialist keeps its own instructions and tools.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.5: "Develop advanced GenAI applications to implement sophisticated AI capabilities"

Sources:

  • Introducing Strands Agents 1.0: Production-Ready Multi-Agent Orchestration Made Simple

INCORRECT: Use a model to classify each message, send the message to the one specialist agent that fits best, and send the reply of that agent to the customer.
This design sends each message to exactly one specialist. The washer message needs the warranty agent and the order agent, so one specialist cannot answer the whole message.

INCORRECT: Create a graph that runs the warranty agent, the order agent and the repair agent in a fixed order for every message, and send the output of the last agent as the reply.
A graph follows a path that the team defines in advance. This graph runs all three agents for every message, also for the messages that need only one specialist. Each message must use only the specialists that it needs.

INCORRECT: Create one agent that has the tools of all three specialists, and put the instructions of all three specialists in its system prompt.
This is the design that failed in the test. A single agent with all the tools and all the instructions often chose the wrong tool.

questions.promptHtml:
A developer at a car rental company works on an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. In the Lambda console, the developer tries to add an Amazon SQS queue as a trigger for the function. The console shows an error message and does not save the trigger.
The developer does not know which permission or setting is wrong. The developer wants the likely cause of the error and the steps to fix it, with the LEAST effort.
Which approach should the developer use?
questions.promptText:
A developer at a car rental company works on an AWS Lambda function that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock. In the Lambda console, the developer tries to add an Amazon SQS queue as a trigger for the function. The console shows an error message and does not save the trigger.
The developer does not know which permission or setting is wrong. The developer wants the likely cause of the error and the steps to fix it, with the LEAST effort.
Which approach should the developer use?

options.text: Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the log group of the function to find error messages from the time of the failure.
Turn on AWS X-Ray active tracing for the function, and read the trace of the failed request to find the missing permission.
Search the AWS CloudTrail event history for the failed request, and compare the IAM policies of the function role with the actions that the request needs.
Choose Diagnose with Amazon Q in the error message, read the explanation of the error, and follow the steps that Amazon Q gives to resolve it.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Choose Diagnose with Amazon Q in the error message, read the explanation of the error, and follow the steps that Amazon Q gives to resolve it.
When Amazon Q can help with a console error, a Diagnose with Amazon Q button appears in the error message. Amazon Q first explains the error, and then it gives steps to resolve it. It diagnoses common errors such as insufficient permissions and incorrect configuration, and AWS Lambda is one of the services that it supports. The developer needs one choice in the error message, so this approach takes the least effort.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 2.5.6: "Improve troubleshooting efficiency for FM applications"

Sources:

  • Diagnosing common errors in the console with Amazon Q Developer
  • Unlocking AWS Console: Diagnosing Errors with Amazon Q Developer

INCORRECT: Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the log group of the function to find error messages from the time of the failure.
The log group stores the logs that the function writes when it runs. The error happened when the console tried to save the trigger, and the function did not run. The log group has no record of this error.

INCORRECT: Turn on AWS X-Ray active tracing for the function, and read the trace of the failed request to find the missing permission.
X-Ray traces requests that the function serves. No request reached the function, because the error happened when the console tried to save the trigger, so there is no trace to read.

INCORRECT: Search the AWS CloudTrail event history for the failed request, and compare the IAM policies of the function role with the actions that the request needs.
This approach can find the cause, but the developer must find the event, read the policies and work out the missing action by hand. It also checks only the function role, and the developer does not know whether a permission or a setting is wrong. Diagnose with Amazon Q gives the cause and the steps with much less effort.

An online marketplace lets sellers upload a photo and a short text for each item. A model in Amazon Bedrock writes the listing from both. Before each model call, the application sends the text and the photo to the ApplyGuardrail API. The team created the guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console with content filters for hate, insults and violence at High strength, and kept the other default settings.
Some violent photos passed the check and appeared in listings. The text with these photos was harmless. The photos are JPEG files under 2 MB.
Which change blocks these photos with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Edit the content filters of the guardrail, and select the image option next to the text option for the hate, insults and violence categories.
Edit the content filters of the guardrail, and add the misconduct category at High strength next to the hate, insults and violence categories.
Add an AWS Lambda function that sends each photo to Amazon Rekognition content moderation, and block the listing when Rekognition returns a moderation label.
Add an instruction to the prompt that tells the model to refuse to write a listing when the photo shows violence.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Edit the content filters of the guardrail, and select the image option next to the text option for the hate, insults and violence categories.
Guardrail content filters can check images as well as text. In the console, the text option is on by default, and the image option must be selected. After this change, the guardrail checks the photo in each ApplyGuardrail call with the same filter strength as the text. The guardrail supports PNG and JPEG images up to 4 MB, so the marketplace's photos fit.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.1: "Develop comprehensive content safety systems to protect against harmful user inputs to FMs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content"

Sources:

  • Block harmful images with content filters
  • Moderating content

INCORRECT: Edit the content filters of the guardrail, and add the misconduct category at High strength next to the hate, insults and violence categories.
This option adds a category, but it does not select the image option. With only the text option, the filters check the text and not the photo. The violent photos came with harmless text, so they would still pass.

INCORRECT: Add an AWS Lambda function that sends each photo to Amazon Rekognition content moderation, and block the listing when Rekognition returns a moderation label.
Amazon Rekognition can detect content that is inappropriate, unwanted or offensive in images. This design adds a Lambda function and a second service that the team must build and maintain. The guardrail that the team already uses can check the photos after one setting change, which has less operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Add an instruction to the prompt that tells the model to refuse to write a listing when the photo shows violence.
The guardrail check runs before the model call, so a prompt instruction does not change what the guardrail blocks. A model also might not follow an instruction every time, so this change does not reliably stop violent photos.

Many upset customers use mildly rude words, and the guardrail blocks their messages. Guardrail traces rate these messages LOW or MEDIUM confidence for insults, and they rate abusive messages HIGH confidence. questions.promptText:
An airline runs a customer service assistant on Amazon Bedrock with one guardrail. The insults content filter uses High strength for prompts and for model responses.
Many upset customers use mildly rude words, and the guardrail blocks their messages. Guardrail traces rate these messages LOW or MEDIUM confidence for insults, and they rate abusive messages HIGH confidence. The airline wants upset customers to receive help, and the guardrail must still block abusive messages. The filter on model responses must stay as strict as it is now.
Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the strength of the insults filter to Medium for prompts, and keep High strength for model responses.
Set the strength of the insults filter to Low for both prompts and model responses.
Set the strength of the insults filter to Low for prompts, and keep High strength for model responses.
Set the action of the insults filter for prompts to NONE, so that the filter only reports detections in the trace, and keep High strength for model responses.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Set the strength of the insults filter to Low for prompts, and keep High strength for model responses.
A guardrail sets the content filter strength for prompts and for model responses separately. At Low strength, a filter blocks only content that it classifies as harmful with HIGH confidence. The mildly rude messages, rated LOW or MEDIUM, now pass, and the guardrail still blocks the abusive messages, rated HIGH. The model responses keep High strength, which blocks insults with LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH confidence.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.2: "Create content safety frameworks to prevent harmful outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter responses"

Sources:

  • Configure content filters for Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • GuardrailContentFilterConfig

INCORRECT: Set the strength of the insults filter to Medium for prompts, and keep High strength for model responses.
Medium strength blocks content that the filter classifies as harmful with HIGH or MEDIUM confidence. The guardrail would still block the upset customers whose messages have MEDIUM confidence.

INCORRECT: Set the strength of the insults filter to Low for both prompts and model responses.
This setting helps the upset customers, but it also weakens the filter on model responses. Responses with insults that have LOW or MEDIUM confidence would reach customers, and the filter on model responses must stay as strict as it is now.

INCORRECT: Set the action of the insults filter for prompts to NONE, so that the filter only reports detections in the trace, and keep High strength for model responses.
With the action NONE, the filter takes no action on prompts and only returns the detection in the trace. The abusive messages would pass too, and the guardrail must still block them.

questions.promptText:
A company's engineers ask a chat assistant about internal design standards. An AWS Lambda function retrieves passages from an Amazon OpenSearch Service index and sends them with the question to a model in Amazon Bedrock. Engineers ask follow-up questions in the same chat, and many answers are longer than 6,000 characters.
Some answers include rules that are in no standard. Before an engineer sees an answer, the team must check it against the retrieved passages. A reviewer must receive each answer that has unsupported parts and see which parts they are.
Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an embedding of each sentence of the answer and of the engineer's question with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. Send the answer to review with each sentence whose similarity to the question is below a set threshold.

Create an embedding of each sentence of the answer and of each retrieved passage with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. Send the answer to review with each sentence whose highest similarity to any passage is below a set threshold.
Set the temperature to 0 in each model call. Add a rule to the system prompt that tells the model to use only the retrieved passages and to say when the passages do not answer the question.

Add a contextual grounding check to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail. Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the retrieved passages as the grounding source and the answer as the content, and send each answer that the check blocks to review.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an embedding of each sentence of the answer and of each retrieved passage with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. Send the answer to review with each sentence whose highest similarity to any passage is below a set threshold.
This option checks each sentence on its own. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings turns a piece of text, such as a sentence or a passage, into a vector, and the vectors can be compared for semantic similarity. A sentence that is close to none of the retrieved passages is likely to have no support in the text that the model received, so a person checks it.

The Lambda function runs this check before the engineer sees the answer, and the reviewer receives the exact sentences to look at. The check works the same way for a long answer and for an answer in a chat.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.3: "Develop accuracy verification systems to reduce hallucinations in FM responses"
Example: "confidence scoring and semantic similarity search for verification"

Sources:

  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings models
  • Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses

INCORRECT: Create an embedding of each sentence of the answer and of the engineer's question with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. Send the answer to review with each sentence whose similarity to the question is below a set threshold.
This option uses the same embeddings, but it compares each sentence with the question, not with the retrieved passages. Similarity to the question shows whether a sentence is on topic. A rule that appears in no standard can still be close to the question, so this check would let that rule pass. The company needs each answer checked against the passages that were retrieved for it.

INCORRECT: Set the temperature to 0 in each model call. Add a rule to the system prompt that tells the model to use only the retrieved passages and to say when the passages do not answer the question.
A low temperature makes the output less random, and the rule in the system prompt asks the model to stay with the passages. Both can lower the number of rules that appear in no standard, but neither one checks an answer. The model might not follow the rule every time, and nothing sends an answer to a reviewer or shows which part has no support.

INCORRECT: Add a contextual grounding check to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail. Call the ApplyGuardrail API with the retrieved passages as the grounding source and the answer as the content, and send each answer that the check blocks to review.
A contextual grounding check compares a model response with a grounding source and gives confidence scores for each response. It does not fit this assistant for three reasons. AWS supports the check for summarization, paraphrasing and question answering, but not for conversational question answering or chatbots, and these engineers ask follow-up questions in the same chat. The check accepts a response of at most 5,000 characters, and many answers are longer.

The score is for the whole response, so the reviewer would not see which part has no support.

questions.promptHtml:
An online learning company runs a study assistant. Learners type short questions in English, and some type insults and threats. An AWS Lambda function sends each question to a model in Amazon Bedrock with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that has content filters. Answers must link only to the company's own course pages.
The security team wants two more checks, separate from the guardrail: one on the learner's text before the model call, and one on the answer before the learner sees it.
Which actions should the team take?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
An online learning company runs a study assistant. Learners type short questions in English, and some type insults and threats. An AWS Lambda function sends each question to a model in Amazon Bedrock with an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that has content filters. Answers must link only to the company's own course pages.
The security team wants two more checks, separate from the guardrail: one on the learner's text before the model call, and one on the answer before the learner sees it.
Which actions should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Raise the strength of the content filters in the guardrail to High for both prompts and responses.
Send the learner's text to the Amazon Comprehend DetectToxicContent API before the model call, and stop the request when the toxicity score is above a set limit.
Send the learner's text to Amazon Comprehend PII detection before the model call, and stop the request when the text contains personal data, such as a name or an address.
Add a rule to the system prompt that tells the model to refuse insults and threats and to link only to the company's course pages.
Check each answer in the Lambda function after the model call, and block the answer when it has a link to a page outside the company's course site.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Send the learner's text to the Amazon Comprehend DetectToxicContent API before the model call, and stop the request when the toxicity score is above a set limit.
Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection checks text for toxic content, such as insults, harassment and threats, and returns a toxicity score for each text string. It supports only English, and each text string can be at most 1 KB. The learners type short questions in English, so this check fits. The Lambda function calls the DetectToxicContent API before the model call and stops the request when the score is above the limit that the team sets. The check runs apart from the guardrail.

CORRECT: Check each answer in the Lambda function after the model call, and block the answer when it has a link to a page outside the company's course site.
A Lambda function can run any check in code after the model call and before the answer reaches the learner. Here the function reads each link in the answer and blocks the answer when a link points outside the course site. This post-processing check does not depend on the model or on the guardrail.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.4: "Create defense-in-depth safety systems to provide comprehensive protection against FM misuse"
Example: "Lambda functions to perform post-processing validation"

Sources:

  • DetectToxicContent
  • Block harmful words and conversations with content filters
  • Detecting PII entities

INCORRECT: Raise the strength of the content filters in the guardrail to High for both prompts and responses.
The content filters of a guardrail have the strengths None, Low, Medium and High, which the team can set apart for prompts and for responses. A higher strength makes the existing guardrail stricter, but it adds no check that is separate from the guardrail. The security team asked for two checks apart from the guardrail, and this change also does not check the links in the answers.

INCORRECT: Send the learner's text to Amazon Comprehend PII detection before the model call, and stop the request when the text contains personal data, such as a name or an address.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection finds personal data, such as names and addresses, in text. The problem in this assistant is insults and threats, not personal data. A question with an insult and no personal data would pass this check.

INCORRECT: Add a rule to the system prompt that tells the model to refuse insults and threats and to link only to the company's course pages.
A rule in the system prompt asks the model to refuse insults and to use only course links. The model might not follow the rule every time, so this is not a separate check. Nothing outside the model looks at the learner's text or at the links in the answer.

An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API and returns each tool result in a toolResult block. The agent has four tools: search hotels, read supplier web pages, send emails and read the full customer table.
Last week, hidden text in a supplier page told the agent to email the customer list to an outside address, and the agent tried to do it. The team must make it much harder for text in tool results to act as instructions, and must limit what the agent can do if such text passes.
Which actions should the team take?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A travel company's hotel agent answers traveler questions about hotels. An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API and returns each tool result in a toolResult block. The agent has four tools: search hotels, read supplier web pages, send emails and read the full customer table.
Last week, hidden text in a supplier page told the agent to email the customer list to an outside address, and the agent tried to do it. The team must make it much harder for text in tool results to act as instructions, and must limit what the agent can do if such text passes.
Which actions should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Wrap all of the agent's instructions in one tag whose name contains a salted sequence that changes in each session, and tell the model to follow only the instructions inside that tag.
Turn on the prompt attack filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail for each Converse call, so that the filter checks the tool results for hidden instructions.
Move the agent to a larger model in Amazon Bedrock, because a larger model follows the instructions in the system prompt more closely.
Remove the email tool and the customer table tool from the agent, and limit the agent's IAM role to the actions that the two remaining tools need.
Turn on model invocation logging, and have the security team review the logged tool results each week for hidden instructions.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Wrap all of the agent's instructions in one tag whose name contains a salted sequence that changes in each session, and tell the model to follow only the instructions inside that tag.
Salted tags keep the real instructions apart from all other text in the prompt. The team puts every instruction in one tag whose name contains a random sequence that changes in each session, and tells the model to follow only the instructions inside that tag. Text in a supplier page cannot copy a tag that it does not know. This makes the model much less likely to follow text from the page as instructions.

CORRECT: Remove the email tool and the customer table tool from the agent, and limit the agent's IAM role to the actions that the two remaining tools need.
An agent should have only the tools and permissions that its task needs. This agent answers questions about hotels, so it needs the hotel search and the supplier pages. Without the email tool and without access to the customer table, hidden text in a page cannot make the agent send the customer list, even when the model follows that text.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.1.5: "Implement advanced threat detection to protect against adversarial inputs and security vulnerabilities"

Sources:

  • Detect prompt attacks with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
  • Best practices to avoid prompt injection attacks
  • Security best practices in IAM

INCORRECT: Turn on the prompt attack filter in an Amazon Bedrock guardrail for each Converse call, so that the filter checks the tool results for hidden instructions.
The prompt attack filter of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails detects jailbreaks and prompt injection in user input. It does not evaluate tool results: the content in toolResult blocks is not checked for prompt attacks. The hidden text was in the result of the supplier page tool, in a toolResult block, so this filter would not see it.

INCORRECT: Move the agent to a larger model in Amazon Bedrock, because a larger model follows the instructions in the system prompt more closely.
A larger model is not a control that keeps instructions apart from data. It could still follow text in a tool result. The agent would also keep the email tool and access to the full customer table, so the same attack could still reach the customer list.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging, and have the security team review the logged tool results each week for hidden instructions.
Model invocation logging records the requests and responses of model calls, and a weekly review could find hidden text later. It does not stop anything at the time of the call. The agent could still follow the hidden text and send the email days before the review.

questions.promptHtml:
A payments company fine-tunes a model with Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs that run in private subnets of a VPC. The subnets have no route to the internet and must keep it that way. The jobs fail because they cannot reach the training data in an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region.
Nobody may read the training data from outside this VPC, even with valid credentials for the training role.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A payments company fine-tunes a model with Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs that run in private subnets of a VPC. The subnets have no route to the internet and must keep it that way. The jobs fail because they cannot reach the training data in an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region.
Nobody may read the training data from outside this VPC, even with valid credentials for the training role.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject on the training data unless the aws:SourceIp condition key matches the CIDR range of the private subnets.
Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC, and associate it with the route tables of the private subnets.
Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject on the training data unless the aws:SourceVpce condition key matches the ID of the endpoint.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet, and add a route from the private subnets to the NAT gateway for the traffic to Amazon S3.
Encrypt the training data with an AWS KMS customer managed key, and allow the training role to use the key in the key policy.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC, and associate it with the route tables of the private subnets.
A gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 lets resources in a VPC reach Amazon S3 without an internet gateway or a NAT device. When the team selects the route tables of the private subnets, AWS adds a route that sends Amazon S3 traffic to the endpoint. The training jobs can then read the bucket, and the subnets keep no route to the internet. The endpoint and the bucket are in the same Region, as a gateway endpoint requires.

CORRECT: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject on the training data unless the aws:SourceVpce condition key matches the ID of the endpoint.
The aws:SourceVpce condition key compares the VPC endpoint of a request with the endpoint ID in the policy. A deny statement with this key blocks every read that does not come through the endpoint. A person outside the VPC with valid credentials for the training role would send the request another way, so the bucket denies it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.1: "Develop protected AI environments to ensure comprehensive security for FM deployments"
Example: "VPC endpoints to isolate networks"

Sources:

  • Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3
  • Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies
  • AWS global condition context keys

INCORRECT: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject on the training data unless the aws:SourceIp condition key matches the CIDR range of the private subnets.
This policy has the same deny statement, but it uses another condition key. The aws:SourceIp key is not in the request when the request comes through a VPC endpoint, and AWS says to use a VPC-specific key for those requests. The training jobs read through the endpoint, so this condition cannot check them in the way that the team wants.

INCORRECT: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet, and add a route from the private subnets to the NAT gateway for the traffic to Amazon S3.
A NAT gateway gives the private subnets a path to the internet. The subnets must keep no route to the internet. A NAT gateway also does not stop a person outside the VPC from reading the bucket with valid credentials.

INCORRECT: Encrypt the training data with an AWS KMS customer managed key, and allow the training role to use the key in the key policy.
A customer managed AWS KMS key encrypts the data at rest and controls who can use the key. The training role is allowed to use the key, so anyone with valid credentials for that role could still read and decrypt the data from outside the VPC. This step also gives the jobs no path to the bucket.

A company plans to summarize its internal sales meeting notes with a third-party model in Amazon Bedrock, called on demand. In tests, only this model wrote summaries that the sales managers accepted.
The legal team set two conditions. No prompt or response may be used to train any model, and none may reach the model provider. The company wants to add no service or setting that the conditions do not need.
Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Attach an AI services opt-out policy for Amazon Bedrock to the organization in AWS Organizations, so that the prompts and responses are not used to train the model.
Redact the notes with Amazon Comprehend PII detection before each call, so that no personal data in the notes reaches the model provider.
Create Provisioned Throughput for the chosen model, so that the company receives a dedicated copy of the model that the provider cannot train on.
Call the chosen model on demand as planned, because Amazon Bedrock does not use prompts or responses to train models and does not share them with model providers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Call the chosen model on demand as planned, because Amazon Bedrock does not use prompts or responses to train models and does not share them with model providers.
Amazon Bedrock does not use the inputs or outputs of a model to train Amazon models or third-party models, and it does not share them with model providers. The model providers have no access to the accounts where Amazon Bedrock runs their models, so they cannot see the prompts and responses. On-demand calls to the chosen model meet both conditions of the legal team with no extra service.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.2: "Develop privacy-preserving systems to protect sensitive information during FM interactions"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock native data privacy features"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock FAQs
  • Data protection
  • Opt out from all supported AWS AI services

INCORRECT: Attach an AI services opt-out policy for Amazon Bedrock to the organization in AWS Organizations, so that the prompts and responses are not used to train the model.
AI services opt-out policies in AWS Organizations stop some AWS AI services from using customer content for service improvement. Amazon Bedrock is not on the list of services that these policies support. Amazon Bedrock needs no such policy, because it already does not use prompts or responses to train models.

INCORRECT: Redact the notes with Amazon Comprehend PII detection before each call, so that no personal data in the notes reaches the model provider.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection can find and redact personal data, such as names and addresses, in text. The conditions are about all prompts and responses, not only personal data, and Amazon Bedrock already meets them. Redaction would add a service that the conditions do not need.

INCORRECT: Create Provisioned Throughput for the chosen model, so that the company receives a dedicated copy of the model that the provider cannot train on.
Provisioned Throughput gives a higher level of throughput for a model at a fixed cost. It is a way to add capacity, not a privacy control. On-demand calls already meet both conditions, so this option would add a cost that the conditions do not need.

questions.promptText:
A food delivery company wants a model in Amazon Bedrock to write a monthly report on complaint trends. The complaint records are in Amazon S3. Each record has the customer's name, phone number and address, the complaint text, the city, the category and the date. The report shows how the number of complaints in each city and category changes each month.
The privacy team allows no single customer complaint to reach the model, even with the name and contact details removed.
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Redact the names, phone numbers and addresses in each record with Amazon Comprehend PII detection, and send the redacted records to the model with the report prompt.
Run an Amazon Athena query that counts the complaints by city, category and month, and send only the query result to the model with the report prompt.
Run an Amazon Athena query that selects the complaints of each month without the name, phone number and address columns, and send the query result to the model.
Send the records to the model with a system prompt that tells the model to report only the totals and never to name a customer in the report.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run an Amazon Athena query that counts the complaints by city, category and month, and send only the query result to the model with the report prompt.
Amazon Athena runs standard SQL queries on data in Amazon S3, with no servers to manage. A query that counts the complaints for each city, category and month returns only totals. The model receives the numbers that the trend report needs, and no single complaint, name or address reaches it.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.2.3: "Create privacy-focused AI systems to protect user privacy while maintaining FM utility and effectiveness"
Example: "anonymization strategies for sensitive information"

Sources:

  • What is Amazon Athena?
  • Detecting PII entities

INCORRECT: Redact the names, phone numbers and addresses in each record with Amazon Comprehend PII detection, and send the redacted records to the model with the report prompt.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection can redact personal data, such as names, phone numbers and addresses, in text. Each redacted record is still the complaint of one customer. The privacy team does not allow any single complaint to reach the model, even without the name and contact details.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Athena query that selects the complaints of each month without the name, phone number and address columns, and send the query result to the model.
This query uses the same service, but it returns each complaint as its own row, only without the contact columns. The model would still read every single complaint, which the privacy team does not allow. The report needs only counts, so the counting can happen in the query.

INCORRECT: Send the records to the model with a system prompt that tells the model to report only the totals and never to name a customer in the report.
A rule in the system prompt can shape what the report says, but the model still reads every record, with the names, phone numbers and addresses. The privacy rule is about what reaches the model, not only about what appears in the report.

questions.promptHtml:
A logistics company fine-tunes an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI every two weeks to sort shipping emails. A SageMaker AI pipeline trains each new version and registers it in SageMaker Model Registry.
Last month, an engineer deployed a version before the compliance team reviewed it. Now only versions that a compliance reviewer accepted may reach production, and each decision must be stored with its version. After a reviewer accepts a version, deployment must start with no manual step.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A logistics company fine-tunes an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI every two weeks to sort shipping emails. A SageMaker AI pipeline trains each new version and registers it in SageMaker Model Registry.
Last month, an engineer deployed a version before the compliance team reviewed it. Now only versions that a compliance reviewer accepted may reach production, and each decision must be stored with its version. After a reviewer accepts a version, deployment must start with no manual step.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Store each reviewer decision as a tag on the model artifact in Amazon S3. Have an AWS Lambda function check the tags of new artifacts every hour and deploy each version with the accepted tag to the production endpoint.

Deploy each new version to the production endpoint with SageMaker AI deployment guardrails. Use canary traffic shifting, and roll back automatically when an Amazon CloudWatch alarm goes off during the update.

Register each new version with the status PendingManualApproval. Have the reviewer set each accepted version to Approved, and start the deployment from an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the SageMaker Model Package State Change event with the status Approved.
Register each new version with the status Approved, so that deployment starts as soon as training ends. Have the reviewer set each version that fails the review to Rejected.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Register each new version with the status PendingManualApproval. Have the reviewer set each accepted version to Approved, and start the deployment from an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the SageMaker Model Package State Change event with the status Approved.
SageMaker Model Registry keeps an approval status for each model version: PendingManualApproval, Approved or Rejected. The pipeline registers each version as PendingManualApproval, and the reviewer changes the status to Approved after the review. The registry stores this status with the version. SageMaker AI sends a SageMaker Model Package State Change event to Amazon EventBridge when the status changes, so a rule can start the deployment with no manual step. Only versions that a reviewer set to Approved reach production.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.1: "Develop compliance frameworks to ensure regulatory compliance for FM deployments"

Sources:

  • Update the Approval Status of a Model
  • Events that Amazon SageMaker AI sends to Amazon EventBridge
  • Deployment guardrails for updating models in production

INCORRECT: Store each reviewer decision as a tag on the model artifact in Amazon S3. Have an AWS Lambda function check the tags of new artifacts every hour and deploy each version with the accepted tag to the production endpoint.
Tags on the model artifact in Amazon S3 could record a decision, and a Lambda function could deploy the tagged versions. The team would build and maintain this check itself, and a deployment could wait up to an hour. The registry already stores an approval status with each version, with less operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Deploy each new version to the production endpoint with SageMaker AI deployment guardrails. Use canary traffic shifting, and roll back automatically when an Amazon CloudWatch alarm goes off during the update.
Deployment guardrails control how traffic moves from the current model to a new one, for example with canary traffic shifting, and they roll back when a CloudWatch alarm goes off. They protect against errors that an alarm can measure. They do not check whether a compliance reviewer accepted the version, so a version that no one reviewed could still reach production.

INCORRECT: Register each new version with the status Approved, so that deployment starts as soon as training ends. Have the reviewer set each version that fails the review to Rejected.
This option uses the same approval status, but every version starts as Approved. Each version would reach production before anyone reviews it, and a Rejected status would come only after the deployment. This repeats the problem from last month.

questions.promptHtml:
A bank's call center staff use an assistant that answers questions about product rules. An AWS Lambda function calls the RetrieveAndGenerate API on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which syncs the rule documents from Amazon S3. The function stores each question and answer in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Months later, auditors may ask which rule documents produced a past answer. Today, the team cannot tell them.
Which solution will meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
A bank's call center staff use an assistant that answers questions about product rules. An AWS Lambda function calls the RetrieveAndGenerate API on a knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which syncs the rule documents from Amazon S3. The function stores each question and answer in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Months later, auditors may ask which rule documents produced a past answer. Today, the team cannot tell them.
Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Turn on knowledge base logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and query the logs for the rule documents that each answer used.
Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for the knowledge base, and look up the RetrieveAndGenerate call of each answer when the auditors ask.
In the same DynamoDB item as the answer, save the Amazon S3 location of each retrieved reference from the citations of the RetrieveAndGenerate response.
Register the S3 bucket of the rule documents in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and show the auditors the catalog entry of each document.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the same DynamoDB item as the answer, save the Amazon S3 location of each retrieved reference from the citations of the RetrieveAndGenerate response.
The RetrieveAndGenerate response contains citations. Each citation links a part of the generated answer to the retrieved references that support it, and each reference has a location, such as the Amazon S3 URI of the document. When the function saves these locations in the same DynamoDB item as the answer, the team can later show which documents produced any stored answer.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.2: "Implement data source tracking to maintain traceability in GenAI applications"

Sources:

  • RetrieveAndGenerate
  • Monitor knowledge bases using CloudWatch Logs
  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail

INCORRECT: Turn on knowledge base logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and query the logs for the rule documents that each answer used.
Knowledge base logging sends logs about data ingestion jobs to CloudWatch Logs, such as the status of each file during a sync. It does not record which documents the knowledge base retrieved for an answer, so these logs cannot link an answer to its documents.

INCORRECT: Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for the knowledge base, and look up the RetrieveAndGenerate call of each answer when the auditors ask.
CloudTrail can log Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate calls as data events for the knowledge base. A CloudTrail event shows who called the API and when. It does not contain the answer and the documents behind it, so the auditors still could not see which documents produced an answer.

INCORRECT: Register the S3 bucket of the rule documents in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and show the auditors the catalog entry of each document.
The AWS Glue Data Catalog keeps a searchable list of data sources and their metadata. It shows which documents exist, but it does not link a single answer to the documents that produced it.

questions.promptHtml:
A company uses AWS Organizations with 35 member accounts, and new accounts join each month. Teams in many accounts build applications on Amazon Bedrock. Administrators of member accounts have full access to their own accounts.
The governance team must review the Amazon Bedrock API activity of every account, such as model calls and guardrail changes, in one Amazon S3 bucket in its log archive account. Administrators of member accounts must not be able to stop or change this logging.
Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A company uses AWS Organizations with 35 member accounts, and new accounts join each month. Teams in many accounts build applications on Amazon Bedrock. Administrators of member accounts have full access to their own accounts.
The governance team must review the Amazon Bedrock API activity of every account, such as model calls and guardrail changes, in one Amazon S3 bucket in its log archive account. Administrators of member accounts must not be able to stop or change this logging.
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a CloudTrail trail to each member account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and automatic deployment, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.
Create an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail from the management account, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each member account that sends Amazon Bedrock API events to an event bus in the log archive account.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each member account, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail from the management account, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.
An organization trail logs events for the management account and for all member accounts. When a new account joins the organization, logging starts for that account automatically. Users in member accounts can see the trail, but they cannot delete it, turn logging on or off, or change it. CloudTrail logs Amazon Bedrock calls such as InvokeModel and Converse as management events, which trails log by default, so the model calls and the guardrail changes reach the central bucket.
