Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.3: "Create organizational governance systems to ensure consistent oversight of FM implementations"

Sources:

  • Creating a trail for an organization
  • Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

INCORRECT: Deploy a CloudTrail trail to each member account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and automatic deployment, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.
StackSets with automatic deployment would also add a trail to each new account. Each trail would still belong to its member account, where the administrators have full access. They could stop the logging or change the trail, which the governance team does not allow.

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each member account that sends Amazon Bedrock API events to an event bus in the log archive account.
An EventBridge rule in a member account can send events to another account. The administrators of each member account have full access, so they could delete or change the rule. The team would also have to add a rule to every new account.

INCORRECT: Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging in each member account, with the bucket in the log archive account as the destination.
Model invocation logging records the requests and responses of model calls, but it supports only destinations in the same account and Region. It cannot write to a bucket in the log archive account. It also does not log other API activity, such as guardrail changes, and the administrators of each account could turn it off.

questions.promptHtml:
A telecom company's chat assistant answers questions about phone plans and can offer account credits. Model invocation logging sends the logs of the assistant's model calls in Amazon Bedrock to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each night, a job reads these logs and checks whether an answer promised a credit above the limit of the customer's plan, which is stored in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
The compliance team now wants each answer checked within 5 minutes, with an alert for each violation.
Which combination of steps will meet the new requirement?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A telecom company's chat assistant answers questions about phone plans and can offer account credits. Model invocation logging sends the logs of the assistant's model calls in Amazon Bedrock to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each night, a job reads these logs and checks whether an answer promised a credit above the limit of the customer's plan, which is stored in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
The compliance team now wants each answer checked within 5 minutes, with an alert for each violation.
Which combination of steps will meet the new requirement?
Select TWO.

options.text: Run the nightly job every hour with an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule, and send an alert through Amazon SNS for each violation that the job finds.
Add Amazon CloudWatch Logs as a second destination of model invocation logging, next to the S3 bucket.
Create a metric filter on the invocation log group that counts the answers with the word "credit", and set an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on that metric.

Create a subscription filter on the invocation log group that sends each new log event to an AWS Lambda function, which checks the credit against the plan limit in DynamoDB and sends an alert through Amazon SNS.
Send the AWS CloudTrail events of the model calls to CloudWatch Logs, and check each event in an AWS Lambda function against the plan limits.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add Amazon CloudWatch Logs as a second destination of model invocation logging, next to the S3 bucket.
Model invocation logging can send logs to Amazon S3, to CloudWatch Logs or to both. With CloudWatch Logs added, the S3 bucket stays, and each model call also arrives in a log group as a log event, with the input and output bodies up to 100 KB. A subscription filter can then read these log events as they arrive.

CORRECT: Create a subscription filter on the invocation log group that sends each new log event to an AWS Lambda function, which checks the credit against the plan limit in DynamoDB and sends an alert through Amazon SNS.
A subscription filter sends log events from a log group to a destination such as an AWS Lambda function, usually less than three minutes after CloudWatch Logs receives them. The function reads the answer in each event, looks up the plan limit in DynamoDB and sends an alert through Amazon SNS. So each answer is usually checked well within the 5 minutes that the compliance team allows.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.3.4: "Implement continuous monitoring and advanced governance controls to support safety audits and regulatory readiness"
Example: "automated detection for misuse, drift, and policy violations"

Sources:

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Real-time processing of log data with subscriptions
  • Creating metrics from log events using filters

INCORRECT: Run the nightly job every hour with an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedule, and send an alert through Amazon SNS for each violation that the job finds.
An hourly schedule makes the job run more often, but a violation could still wait close to an hour for the next run. The compliance team wants each answer checked within 5 minutes.

INCORRECT: Create a metric filter on the invocation log group that counts the answers with the word "credit", and set an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on that metric.
A metric filter turns log data that matches a pattern into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm can watch that metric. It can count the answers that contain the word "credit", but it cannot compare the amount in an answer with the limit of the customer's plan in DynamoDB. Every answer that mentions a credit would count, allowed or not.

INCORRECT: Send the AWS CloudTrail events of the model calls to CloudWatch Logs, and check each event in an AWS Lambda function against the plan limits.
CloudTrail records each Converse or InvokeModel call as a management event, which shows who called the API and when. The event does not contain the answer text, so the function would have no credit amount to check.

questions.promptHtml:
An online marketplace checks each new seller listing against its listing rules with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The application calls the Converse API with structured outputs, and the JSON schema has one field, decision, with the value approve or reject. The application publishes or blocks each listing based on this field.
Many sellers with blocked listings ask the support team what to change. Each seller must now see a short reason in plain words next to the decision, and the reason must name the broken rule. The application must keep reading the decision from the same field.
How should the team meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online marketplace checks each new seller listing against its listing rules with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The application calls the Converse API with structured outputs, and the JSON schema has one field, decision, with the value approve or reject. The application publishes or blocks each listing based on this field.
Many sellers with blocked listings ask the support team what to change. Each seller must now see a short reason in plain words next to the decision, and the reason must name the broken rule. The application must keep reading the decision from the same field.
How should the team meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a reason field to the JSON schema with a maxLength of 200 characters and a description that asks for the broken rule, and show the reason to the seller with the decision.
Remove the JSON schema, and ask the model in the prompt to answer in free text, with the decision on the first line and a short reason that names the broken rule on the next line.
Add a reason field to the JSON schema, ask the model in the prompt for one or two plain sentences that name the broken rule, and show the reason to the seller with the decision.
Keep the JSON schema as it is, and show every blocked seller a help page that lists each listing rule with a short explanation and an example.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add a reason field to the JSON schema, ask the model in the prompt for one or two plain sentences that name the broken rule, and show the reason to the seller with the decision.
Structured outputs make the model response follow the JSON schema that the application sends. A new reason field next to the decision field gives each response two parts: the decision that the application reads, and a short text for the seller. The model writes both parts in the same response, so the reason explains the decision that it belongs to.

The prompt sets the length and the plain words, and the application shows the reason with the decision.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.1: "Develop transparent AI systems in FM outputs"

Sources:

  • Get validated JSON results from models
  • Converse

INCORRECT: Add a reason field to the JSON schema with a maxLength of 200 characters and a description that asks for the broken rule, and show the reason to the seller with the decision.
This option adds the same reason field, and it limits the length in the schema. Structured outputs in Amazon Bedrock support only part of JSON Schema, and string constraints such as maxLength are not supported. A schema with a feature that is not supported returns a 400 error, so every request would fail and no listing would receive a decision.

INCORRECT: Remove the JSON schema, and ask the model in the prompt to answer in free text, with the decision on the first line and a short reason that names the broken rule on the next line.
Free text has no fixed fields, and structured outputs no longer check the format of the response. The application must keep reading the decision from the same field, and a line of free text is not that field. A small change in the wording of the model could also break the step that publishes or blocks the listing.

INCORRECT: Keep the JSON schema as it is, and show every blocked seller a help page that lists each listing rule with a short explanation and an example.
A help page with every rule gives general advice, and it is the same for every seller. It does not say which rule this listing breaks. The requirement is a reason for each decision that names the broken rule, so the seller would still have to guess.

questions.promptHtml:
An online learning company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to give feedback on student essays. Before each release, an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a model as judge scores the feedback for 900 test essays. Each test essay record shows the first language of its student. The latest overall score passes the release bar.
Before each release, the company must show that the feedback is equally good for students of every first language.
What should the team change in the evaluation?
questions.promptText:
An online learning company uses a model in Amazon Bedrock to give feedback on student essays. Before each release, an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job with a model as judge scores the feedback for 900 test essays. Each test essay record shows the first language of its student. The latest overall score passes the release bar.
Before each release, the company must show that the feedback is equally good for students of every first language.
What should the team change in the evaluation?

options.text: Rebuild the test set with the same number of essays for each first language, and release when the overall score of the job passes the bar.
Add the first language of each essay as the category key of its prompt in the evaluation dataset, and compare the scores that the job reports for each category.
Remove the first language from every test essay record before the job runs, so that the judge model cannot score the feedback of any group in a different way.
Raise the release bar for the overall score, so that each release needs a higher average score for the 900 test essays.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the first language of each essay as the category key of its prompt in the evaluation dataset, and compare the scores that the job reports for each category.
The prompt dataset of an evaluation job with a model as judge has an optional category key. When each prompt has a category, the job reports the evaluation scores for each category. With the first language as the category, the team sees one score for each group and can compare the groups before the release. An overall score is an average, and a high average can hide one group whose feedback is worse.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.2: "Apply fairness evaluations to ensure unbiased FM outputs"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock with LLM-as-a-judge solutions to perform automated model evaluations"

Sources:

  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge

INCORRECT: Rebuild the test set with the same number of essays for each first language, and release when the overall score of the job passes the bar.
A test set with an equal number of essays for each language is balanced. The job still reports one overall score. One group can receive worse feedback while the other groups raise the average, so this score cannot show that the feedback is equally good for every group.

INCORRECT: Remove the first language from every test essay record before the job runs, so that the judge model cannot score the feedback of any group in a different way.
Removing the first language looks fair, because the judge model no longer sees it. The feedback model still writes feedback for essays from every group, and the team loses the only field that shows which essay belongs to which group. Without this field, the team cannot compare the groups at all.

INCORRECT: Raise the release bar for the overall score, so that each release needs a higher average score for the 900 test essays.
A higher bar asks for better feedback on average. A strong average can still come from most groups doing well and one group doing badly. The company needs to see each group, and one higher number for all essays does not show the groups.

questions.promptHtml:
A retail company fine-tuned an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI to write product descriptions from supplier data. The team built and tested the model for clothing. In a later test on electronics, the model often wrote wrong numbers for sizes and power use.
Other teams find approved models in SageMaker Model Registry and deploy them from there. They never open the model files in Amazon S3. The governance team wants these teams to see what the model is for, and where it fails, before they build on it.
How should the team record this information?
questions.promptText:
A retail company fine-tuned an open-weight model on Amazon SageMaker AI to write product descriptions from supplier data. The team built and tested the model for clothing. In a later test on electronics, the model often wrote wrong numbers for sizes and power use.
Other teams find approved models in SageMaker Model Registry and deploy them from there. They never open the model files in Amazon S3. The governance team wants these teams to see what the model is for, and where it fails, before they build on it.
How should the team record this information?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for electronics products, and ask the other teams to call the ApplyGuardrail API with each request to the model that they deploy.
Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records each deployment of the model from Model Registry, and send the records to the governance team each week for review.
Write the intended uses and the electronics errors in a README file, and store the file in the Amazon S3 folder with the model files.
Complete the model card of the model version in Model Registry, with the intended uses, the uses that are not recommended, and the electronics errors in caveats and recommendations.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Complete the model card of the model version in Model Registry, with the intended uses, the uses that are not recommended, and the electronics errors in caveats and recommendations.
A SageMaker model card documents a model in one place: what it is for, its risk rating, its evaluation results, and notes for the people who use it. Model Registry includes a model card in each registered model version, so the other teams see the card where they already find the model. The intended uses can say that the model fits clothing and is not recommended for electronics.

The caveats and recommendations section is the place for the wrong numbers in the electronics test. A team that reads the card knows the limit before it builds on the model.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 3.4.3: "Develop policy-compliant AI systems to ensure adherence to responsible AI practices"
Example: "model cards to document FM limitations"

Sources:

  • Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
  • Update the Details of a Model Version
  • Block denied topics to help remove harmful content

INCORRECT: Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for electronics products, and ask the other teams to call the ApplyGuardrail API with each request to the model that they deploy.
A denied topic blocks prompts and responses about a topic and returns a blocked message. It acts only when the model runs, after a team has already built on it. It does not tell the teams what the model is for, and it does not explain the wrong numbers.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records each deployment of the model from Model Registry, and send the records to the governance team each week for review.
CloudTrail records API calls, such as who deployed which model and when. The governance team would learn about each deployment after it happened. The other teams would still see nothing about the intended uses or the electronics errors before they build.

INCORRECT: Write the intended uses and the electronics errors in a README file, and store the file in the Amazon S3 folder with the model files.
A README file can contain the same text. The other teams find and deploy models from Model Registry, and they never open the model files in Amazon S3. They would not see the file before they build on the model.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A car parts wholesaler receives about 8,000 order emails each day. An application sends each email to a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API, and the model returns the order as JSON. When a reply is not valid JSON, the application sends the request again.
The team must choose between two models, and one has lower token prices. In a first trial, the two models wrote replies of very different lengths. Staff fix wrong orders by hand, so only correct orders count. The team has 250 past emails with checked orders.
How should the team compare the cost of the two models?
questions.promptText:
A car parts wholesaler receives about 8,000 order emails each day. An application sends each email to a model in Amazon Bedrock with the Converse API, and the model returns the order as JSON. When a reply is not valid JSON, the application sends the request again.
The team must choose between two models, and one has lower token prices. In a first trial, the two models wrote replies of very different lengths. Staff fix wrong orders by hand, so only correct orders count. The team has 250 past emails with checked orders.
How should the team compare the cost of the two models?

options.text: Compare the prices per 1 million input tokens and output tokens of the two models on the Amazon Bedrock pricing page, and choose the model with the lower prices.
Run the application on the 250 emails with each model. Add the cost of the input and output tokens in the usage field of every call, and divide each total by the number of correct orders.
Send the 250 emails to the CountTokens API with each model. Multiply each count by the input token price of that model, and divide each total by the number of correct orders in a trial run.
Set the same maxTokens value for both models, so that the replies have similar lengths. Then run the 250 emails with each model, and compare the total token cost of the two runs.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run the application on the 250 emails with each model. Add the cost of the input and output tokens in the usage field of every call, and divide each total by the number of correct orders.
This comparison measures what the company pays for useful work. Amazon Bedrock prices on-demand calls by input tokens and output tokens, and the usage field of each Converse response gives both counts for that call.

Because the team runs the application itself, the calls also include the retries that the application sends after a reply that is not valid JSON, and the team adds the usage of every call. Dividing by the number of correct orders gives the cost of each order that counts. A model with lower token prices can still cost more for each correct order when it writes longer replies, needs more retries or makes more mistakes.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.2: "Create cost-effective model selection frameworks"
Example: "price-to-performance ratio measurement"

Sources:

  • Amazon Bedrock pricing
  • Converse
  • Monitor your token usage by counting tokens before running inference

INCORRECT: Compare the prices per 1 million input tokens and output tokens of the two models on the Amazon Bedrock pricing page, and choose the model with the lower prices.
The pricing page lists a price per 1 million input tokens and a price per 1 million output tokens for each model. A price per token does not show how many tokens each model uses for an order, or how many of its orders are correct. In the trial, the two models wrote replies of very different lengths, and invalid replies lead to retries, so the model with the lower prices can be the more expensive one for this work.

INCORRECT: Send the 250 emails to the CountTokens API with each model. Multiply each count by the input token price of that model, and divide each total by the number of correct orders in a trial run.
Here, the method counts the correct orders, which matters, so it is close to the right method. However, the CountTokens API returns only the number of input tokens that a request would use, and it does not charge for the count. The method does not count the output tokens, where the trial showed very different lengths. It also counts each email once, so it does not count the retries that the application sends after a reply that is not valid JSON.

INCORRECT: Set the same maxTokens value for both models, so that the replies have similar lengths. Then run the 250 emails with each model, and compare the total token cost of the two runs.
Setting maxTokens in the inference configuration of a Converse call limits the length of the reply. When a reply reaches the limit, the model stops, and the response shows the stop reason max_tokens. An order that stops early is not valid JSON, so this setting can add retries. The method also compares only the total cost of each run, and it never counts how many orders are correct.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A payments company runs a fraud review assistant that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock all day, every day. The steady load is about 300,000 input and 30,000 output tokens per minute. A few times each week, the load doubles for about an hour. The model supports the Reserved tier, and the on-demand quota of the account covers the extra load in those hours.
The steady load must have capacity that is set aside for the company. Requests in the busy hours must still be served.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
questions.promptText:
A payments company runs a fraud review assistant that calls a model in Amazon Bedrock all day, every day. The steady load is about 300,000 input and 30,000 output tokens per minute. A few times each week, the load doubles for about an hour. The model supports the Reserved tier, and the on-demand quota of the account covers the extra load in those hours.
The steady load must have capacity that is set aside for the company. Requests in the busy hours must still be served.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity in the Reserved tier for the doubled load, so that the reservation also covers the busy hours.
Send every request with the service_tier parameter set to priority, so that Amazon Bedrock serves the assistant before Standard and Flex requests.
Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity in the Reserved tier for the steady load, and let requests above the reservation overflow to the Standard tier.
Send the steady load in the Flex tier for its discount, and send the requests of the busy hours in the Priority tier for faster responses.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity in the Reserved tier for the steady load, and let requests above the reservation overflow to the Standard tier.
The Reserved tier sets aside tokens-per-minute capacity for input and output, for a fixed price that is billed monthly. When the application needs more than the reservation, Amazon Bedrock sends the extra requests to the Standard tier, where the on-demand quota of the account serves them. A reservation for the steady load gives the capacity that is set aside, and the company pays the Standard price only for the extra load in the busy hours.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.1.3: "Develop high-performance FM systems to maximize resource utilization and throughput for GenAI workloads"
Example: "capacity planning"

Sources:

  • Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost
  • Amazon Bedrock Pricing

INCORRECT: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity in the Reserved tier for the doubled load, so that the reservation also covers the busy hours.
A reservation for the doubled load also sets capacity aside, and it serves the busy hours. The company pays the fixed price for all of that capacity for the whole month, but it uses half of it only a few hours each week. The reservation for the steady load meets the same requirements for less.

INCORRECT: Send every request with the service_tier parameter set to priority, so that Amazon Bedrock serves the assistant before Standard and Flex requests.
The Priority tier serves requests before Standard and Flex requests, for a price above the Standard price. It needs no reservation and uses the on-demand quota of the account, so no capacity is set aside for the company. The company would also pay the higher price for every request.

INCORRECT: Send the steady load in the Flex tier for its discount, and send the requests of the busy hours in the Priority tier for faster responses.
The Flex tier gives a discount for workloads that can wait longer for a response, and the Priority tier costs more than Standard. Neither tier sets capacity aside, because both use the on-demand quota of the account. A fraud review assistant that runs all day needs the steady capacity that this option does not give.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's internal assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference. Each weekday at 07:00, a scheduled job uses the same model in the same account and Region to summarize the support cases of the night. The job summarizes about 3,000 cases and ends at about 07:15.
Assistant users see ThrottlingException errors from Amazon Bedrock only between 07:00 and 07:15. Later in the day, the assistant sends more requests and more tokens each minute than at 07:00, and it has no errors. The daily token use of the account stays far below its daily quota.
What is the cause of these errors?
questions.promptText:
A company's internal assistant calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference. Each weekday at 07:00, a scheduled job uses the same model in the same account and Region to summarize the support cases of the night. The job summarizes about 3,000 cases and ends at about 07:15.
Assistant users see ThrottlingException errors from Amazon Bedrock only between 07:00 and 07:15. Later in the day, the assistant sends more requests and more tokens each minute than at 07:00, and it has no errors. The daily token use of the account stays far below its daily quota.
What is the cause of these errors?

options.text: The account uses up its daily token quota for Amazon Bedrock in the Region, and the quota starts again after the job ends.
Some cases of the night are longer than the input limit of the model, so Amazon Bedrock rejects the requests of the job.
The assistant traffic at 07:00 alone passes the per-minute quota of the model in the account and Region, because many users start the day with long chats and long questions.
The job sends many model calls in the same minutes, and together with the assistant calls they pass the per-minute quota of the model in the account and Region.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The job sends many model calls in the same minutes, and together with the assistant calls they pass the per-minute quota of the model in the account and Region.
Amazon Bedrock limits the tokens that an account can use for each model in each Region in one minute, with input and output counted together, and for some models it also limits the requests in one minute. The job finishes about 3,000 summaries in 15 minutes, so it sends many calls in each of those minutes. The assistant shares the same quota, and the total passes it. Amazon Bedrock then returns ThrottlingException, the error for requests over the account quotas.

When the job ends, the load falls under the quota, and the errors stop. A limit on how many calls the job runs at the same time fixes the problem with no change to the assistant.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.3: "Implement FM throughput optimization to address the specific throughput challenges of GenAI workloads"
Example: "concurrent model invocation management"

Sources:

  • Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint
  • Troubleshooting Amazon Bedrock API Error Codes

INCORRECT: The account uses up its daily token quota for Amazon Bedrock in the Region, and the quota starts again after the job ends.
Amazon Bedrock has a daily token quota for each account in each Region. The account stays far below it. A used-up daily quota would also cause errors for the rest of the day, not only for 15 minutes.

INCORRECT: Some cases of the night are longer than the input limit of the model, so Amazon Bedrock rejects the requests of the job.
A request that is longer than the input limit of the model fails with a validation error, not with ThrottlingException. Such an error would stop only the job request, and the assistant users would not see errors.

INCORRECT: The assistant traffic at 07:00 alone passes the per-minute quota of the model in the account and Region, because many users start the day with long chats and long questions.
Later in the day, the assistant sends more requests and more tokens each minute than at 07:00, and it has no errors. Assistant traffic alone stays under the quota, so it is not the cause. The errors appear only while the job runs.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A travel company writes hotel descriptions for its website with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The application calls the Converse API with a low temperature and a low top P. Editors say that many descriptions sound the same from hotel to hotel.
The team will tune these settings to make the text more varied. Each description must still name only the facilities in the hotel record. The team must know which setting caused each change in the results.
Which steps should the team take?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A travel company writes hotel descriptions for its website with a model in Amazon Bedrock. The application calls the Converse API with a low temperature and a low top P. Editors say that many descriptions sound the same from hotel to hotel.
The team will tune these settings to make the text more varied. Each description must still name only the facilities in the hotel record. The team must know which setting caused each change in the results.
Which steps should the team take?
Select TWO.

options.text: Raise the temperature and top P together in small steps in each test round, so that each round adds a little more variety.
Change only the temperature in each test round, and keep top P at its current value.
Run each test round on a new random set of hotel records, so that the tests cover more hotels over time.
Set top K to 1 through the additional model request fields, so that the model always picks the most likely token and names no facility that is not in the record.
Run each test round on the same fixed set of hotel records, and score every output with the same checks for variety and for facilities that are not in the record.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Change only the temperature in each test round, and keep top P at its current value.
Temperature and top P both change how likely the model is to pick lower-probability tokens. When only one setting changes in a test round, the team can link a change in the results to this one setting. After the temperature tests, the team can test top P in the same way, with the temperature fixed.

CORRECT: Run each test round on the same fixed set of hotel records, and score every output with the same checks for variety and for facilities that are not in the record.
A fixed set of hotel records means that the setting is the only thing that changes between rounds. The same checks score each round for variety and for facilities that the record does not list. The team can then compare the rounds and see whether more variety also brings invented facilities.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.4: "Enhance FM performance to achieve optimal results for specific GenAI use cases"
Example: "appropriate temperature and top-k/top-p selection based on requirements"

Sources:

  • Influence response generation with inference parameters
  • Converse

INCORRECT: Raise the temperature and top P together in small steps in each test round, so that each round adds a little more variety.
Raising both settings gives more variety, and small steps look careful. When both settings change in the same round, the team cannot tell which one caused a better result or a new invented facility. This option fails the requirement to know which setting caused each change.

INCORRECT: Run each test round on a new random set of hotel records, so that the tests cover more hotels over time.
New hotels in each round test more of the hotel list. Some hotel records are easier to describe than others, so the results change with the records as well as with the setting. The team could not tell whether a change came from the setting or from the new records.

INCORRECT: Set top K to 1 through the additional model request fields, so that the model always picks the most likely token and names no facility that is not in the record.
With top K set to 1, the model considers only the most likely next token. This removes variety, which is the opposite of what the editors want. It also does not stop invented facilities, because the most likely token can still name a facility that the record does not list.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's mobile app sends each user question through Amazon API Gateway to an AWS Lambda function in Python. The function creates a boto3 client for Amazon Bedrock Runtime inside its handler, and then calls a model with the Converse API.
AWS X-Ray traces show that every invocation, also on warm execution environments, spends about 250 ms on client setup and a new connection before the model call starts. The team wants to remove this delay from warm invocations with no change to the model.
Which change should the team make?
questions.promptText:
A company's mobile app sends each user question through Amazon API Gateway to an AWS Lambda function in Python. The function creates a boto3 client for Amazon Bedrock Runtime inside its handler, and then calls a model with the Converse API.
AWS X-Ray traces show that every invocation, also on warm execution environments, spends about 250 ms on client setup and a new connection before the model call starts. The team wants to remove this delay from warm invocations with no change to the model.
Which change should the team make?

options.text: Create the boto3 client once in the code outside the handler, so that warm invocations reuse the client and its open connections.
Turn on provisioned concurrency for an alias of the function, so that Lambda prepares execution environments and runs the initialization code before the requests arrive.
Call the model with ConverseStream instead of Converse, so that the app shows the first words of each answer sooner.
Raise the memory setting of the function, so that Lambda gives the function more CPU power for the client setup.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create the boto3 client once in the code outside the handler, so that warm invocations reuse the client and its open connections.
Lambda keeps an execution environment for later invocations, and code outside the handler runs only when the environment starts. A boto3 client created there stays in memory, so each warm invocation reuses the client and its connections. Warm requests then skip the 250 ms of client setup, which runs only once, when each environment starts.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.2.6: "Optimize FM system performance for GenAI workflows"
Example: "efficient service communication patterns"

Sources:

  • Best practices for working with AWS Lambda Event Functions
  • Configuring provisioned concurrency for an Event Function
  • Configure Lambda Event Function memory

INCORRECT: Turn on provisioned concurrency for an alias of the function, so that Lambda prepares execution environments and runs the initialization code before the requests arrive.
Provisioned concurrency prepares execution environments in advance and runs the initialization code before requests arrive. Code inside the handler still runs on every invocation, with or without provisioned concurrency. The client setup stays in each request.

INCORRECT: Call the model with ConverseStream instead of Converse, so that the app shows the first words of each answer sooner.
ConverseStream returns the answer in parts, so users see the first words sooner after the model starts. The function still creates a new client and a new connection in the handler before the call. The 250 ms before the model call stays the same.

INCORRECT: Raise the memory setting of the function, so that Lambda gives the function more CPU power for the client setup.
Lambda gives a function CPU power in proportion to its memory, so the setup may run a little faster. The function still builds a new client and opens a new connection on every invocation. The setup work still runs in each request, so the delay before the model call does not go away.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company runs its generative AI app in three AWS accounts in the same Region. One account runs Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda, one runs the Amazon Bedrock calls and the knowledge base, and one runs the data pipeline. All three accounts send metrics and logs to Amazon CloudWatch and traces to AWS X-Ray.
To follow one slow request, on-call engineers now sign in to each account. They want to search the metrics, logs and traces of all three accounts from one account.
Which solution meets this need?
questions.promptText:
A company runs its generative AI app in three AWS accounts in the same Region. One account runs Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda, one runs the Amazon Bedrock calls and the knowledge base, and one runs the data pipeline. All three accounts send metrics and logs to Amazon CloudWatch and traces to AWS X-Ray.
To follow one slow request, on-call engineers now sign in to each account. They want to search the metrics, logs and traces of all three accounts from one account.
Which solution meets this need?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter in each account that sends every log group of the app to an Amazon Data Firehose stream in one central account for the on-call engineers.
Create an AWS CloudTrail trail in each account that delivers the API events of the account to one Amazon S3 bucket for queries.
Configure CloudWatch cross-account observability with a central monitoring account, and link the three accounts to it as source accounts that share metrics, log groups and traces.
Build a CloudWatch dashboard in each account for its part of the app, and share the three dashboards with the on-call engineers.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Configure CloudWatch cross-account observability with a central monitoring account, and link the three accounts to it as source accounts that share metrics, log groups and traces.
CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to one monitoring account in the same Region. Each source account shares its metrics, log groups and X-Ray traces, and the engineers search and analyze all of them from the monitoring account. The trace of one slow request then shows every part of the app in one place.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.1: "Create holistic observability systems to provide complete visibility into FM application performance"
Example: "performance tracing"

Sources:

  • CloudWatch cross-account observability
  • Log group-level subscription filters

INCORRECT: Create a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter in each account that sends every log group of the app to an Amazon Data Firehose stream in one central account for the on-call engineers.
A subscription filter streams log events from a log group to a destination, such as an Amazon Data Firehose stream. This option moves logs only. The metrics and the X-Ray traces stay in each account, so the engineers still sign in to each account to follow a request.

INCORRECT: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail in each account that delivers the API events of the account to one Amazon S3 bucket for queries.
CloudTrail records the API calls in an account, such as who changed a Lambda function and when. These events do not contain the application metrics, the application logs or the traces of a request. They cannot show where one request became slow.

INCORRECT: Build a CloudWatch dashboard in each account for its part of the app, and share the three dashboards with the on-call engineers.
Each dashboard in this option shows the data of its own account. Three shared dashboards are still three places, and a dashboard is not a search of the logs and traces of all accounts. The engineers would still move from account to account to follow one request.

questions.domain: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
questions.promptHtml:
A company's field service app helps technicians plan repairs with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Each Converse request sends the team ID of the technician as request metadata, and model invocation logging writes every call to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each night, the job system exports the finished repairs to another S3 bucket, with the team ID and whether the first visit fixed the problem.
Leaders want a weekly dashboard that shows, for each team, the use of the app next to the first-visit fix rate.
Which steps meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company's field service app helps technicians plan repairs with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Each Converse request sends the team ID of the technician as request metadata, and model invocation logging writes every call to an Amazon S3 bucket. Each night, the job system exports the finished repairs to another S3 bucket, with the team ID and whether the first visit fixed the problem.
Leaders want a weekly dashboard that shows, for each team, the use of the app next to the first-visit fix rate.
Which steps meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Select TWO.

options.text: Catalog the invocation logs and the repair exports with AWS Glue, and join them on the team ID for each week with a query in Amazon Athena.
Send the invocation logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs as well, and count the requests for each team ID with a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on a dashboard.
Write an AWS Lambda function that runs each week, reads every log file and every export file, counts the results for each team, and writes an HTML report to Amazon S3.
Create an Amazon Quick Sight dataset from the Athena query, and build and share a dashboard with the weekly results for the leaders.
Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job each week on a sample of the logged requests, and send the quality scores of the answers to the leaders.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Catalog the invocation logs and the repair exports with AWS Glue, and join them on the team ID for each week with a query in Amazon Athena.
Model invocation logs in Amazon S3 can be cataloged with AWS Glue and queried with Amazon Athena. Each log record contains the request metadata, so the team ID is in the logs. The repair exports in S3 can be cataloged in the same way, and one SQL query joins the two sources on the team ID for each week. This step uses managed services and needs no code to maintain.

CORRECT: Create an Amazon Quick Sight dataset from the Athena query, and build and share a dashboard with the weekly results for the leaders.
Amazon Quick Sight can create a dataset from Amazon Athena with a custom SQL query. The leaders then see the use of the app and the first-visit fix rate of each team side by side in one dashboard. No servers or report code are needed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.3: "Develop integrated observability solutions to provide actionable insights for FM applications"
Example: "business impact visualizations"

Sources:

  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Creating a dataset using Amazon Athena data

INCORRECT: Send the invocation logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs as well, and count the requests for each team ID with a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on a dashboard.
CloudWatch Logs Insights can count the requests for each team ID, because the request metadata is in each log record. The repair results are not in CloudWatch Logs. The dashboard can show the use of the app, and it cannot show the first-visit fix rate next to it.

INCORRECT: Write an AWS Lambda function that runs each week, reads every log file and every export file, counts the results for each team, and writes an HTML report to Amazon S3.
A weekly Lambda function can read both sources and build the same report. The team must write, test and maintain this code, and change it for each new question from the leaders. AWS Glue, Amazon Athena and Amazon Quick Sight do the same work as managed services with less operational overhead.

INCORRECT: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job each week on a sample of the logged requests, and send the quality scores of the answers to the leaders.
An evaluation job scores the quality of model answers, such as their correctness. It does not show how often each team uses the app, and it does not use the repair results. The leaders want business results next to the use of the app, and answer quality is a different measure.

questions.promptHtml:
A furniture retailer runs a delivery agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent books new delivery days with a book_slot tool.
AgentCore Observability shows sessions with 9 or 10 book_slot calls in a row for the same date and slot, and then no booking. Each call returns in less than a second with {"status": "failed", "code": 409}. The booking API logs show that the warehouse is closed on these dates. Each model call includes all earlier tool calls and results.
What is the cause of the repeated calls?
questions.promptText:
A furniture retailer runs a delivery agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent books new delivery days with a book_slot tool.
AgentCore Observability shows sessions with 9 or 10 book_slot calls in a row for the same date and slot, and then no booking. Each call returns in less than a second with {"status": "failed", "code": 409}. The booking API logs show that the warehouse is closed on these dates. Each model call includes all earlier tool calls and results.
What is the cause of the repeated calls?

options.text: The book_slot tool times out before the booking API answers, so the agent sends the same call again after each timeout.
The book_slot tool definition does not describe the date format, so the agent sends each date in a format that the booking API rejects.
The tool result says that the booking failed but not why, so the agent finds nothing to change and sends the same call again.
The agent loses the earlier tool results between model calls, so it does not know that it already tried this date and slot.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The tool result says that the booking failed but not why, so the agent finds nothing to change and sends the same call again.
The tool result is all that the model learns about a tool call. Here the result holds a status and a code, and nothing in it says that the warehouse is closed on that date. The model cannot read the booking API logs, so it has no reason to choose another day, and it tries the same call again.

With Amazon Bedrock, a tool can send error text back to the model in the tool result. A result such as "The warehouse is closed on this date. Choose another date." gives the agent something to act on.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.4: "Create tool performance frameworks to ensure optimal tool operation and utilization for FMs"
Example: "tool calling observability and multi-agent coordination tracking"

Sources:

  • Call a tool with the Converse API
  • Observe your agent applications on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability

INCORRECT: The book_slot tool times out before the booking API answers, so the agent sends the same call again after each timeout.
A timeout means that a tool runs out of time before it gets an answer. Here each call returns in less than a second, and each call comes back with a result from the booking API. No call timed out.

INCORRECT: The book_slot tool definition does not describe the date format, so the agent sends each date in a format that the booking API rejects.
A tool definition with no date format is a common reason for failed calls, because the model must guess the format. Here the booking API logs show the dates of these calls, and they show that the warehouse is closed on those days. The API read each date correctly, so the format is not the problem.

INCORRECT: The agent loses the earlier tool results between model calls, so it does not know that it already tried this date and slot.
An agent that forgets its earlier tries can repeat a call. The question states the opposite: each model call in the session includes all earlier tool calls and results. The agent sees each failed try, but none of them tells it what to change.

questions.promptHtml:
A gym chain runs a member support agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents, with trace turned on. An AWS Lambda function runs the functions of its action group. The cancel_membership function sends a cancellation form. Last month, the team added pause_membership, which stops payments for a few months.
Since then, some members who ask for a pause receive the cancellation form. In the trace of these sessions, the agent calls only cancel_membership, with the correct member ID, and no step shows an error. A message such as "I want to stop my membership for the summer" gives this result every time. "Please pause my membership" reaches pause_membership.
What is the cause of this issue?
questions.promptText:
A gym chain runs a member support agent in Amazon Bedrock Agents, with trace turned on. An AWS Lambda function runs the functions of its action group. The cancel_membership function sends a cancellation form. Last month, the team added pause_membership, which stops payments for a few months.
Since then, some members who ask for a pause receive the cancellation form. In the trace of these sessions, the agent calls only cancel_membership, with the correct member ID, and no step shows an error. A message such as "I want to stop my membership for the summer" gives this result every time. "Please pause my membership" reaches pause_membership.
What is the cause of this issue?

options.text: The Lambda function returns an error when the agent calls pause_membership, so the agent then calls cancel_membership for the same request.
The team did not prepare the agent after it added pause_membership, so the version that members use does not include the new function.
The descriptions of cancel_membership and pause_membership both say that the function stops a membership, so the model cannot see which function a message needs.
The temperature of the orchestration step is too high, so the model picks one of the two membership functions at random for each request.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: The descriptions of cancel_membership and pause_membership both say that the function stops a membership, so the model cannot see which function a message needs.
The agent predicts which function to call from the member's message and the function definitions. Each definition includes a description of the function and its purpose. If both descriptions say that the function stops a membership, a message with the word "stop" fits both, and the model has no clear reason to choose the new function, so in these sessions it chose cancel_membership. "Please pause my membership" names the new function clearly, so that message works.

The trace helps here, because it shows the prompt that the model reads at each step and the reasoning that the agent uses to choose an action. The fix is a description for each function that names its own job, for example "Stops payments for a set number of months and keeps the membership."

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 4.3.6: "Develop FM-specific troubleshooting frameworks to identify unique GenAI failure modes that are not present in traditional ML systems"
Example: "reasoning path tracing to identify logical errors"

Sources:

  • Track agent's step-by-step reasoning process using trace
  • Test and troubleshoot agent behavior
  • Function

INCORRECT: The Lambda function returns an error when the agent calls pause_membership, so the agent then calls cancel_membership for the same request.
When an error occurs, the trace returns a field with the error message. If calls to pause_membership failed, the trace would show those calls and the errors. The trace shows that the agent called only cancel_membership and that no step has an error, so the agent never tried the pause function in these sessions.

INCORRECT: The team did not prepare the agent after it added pause_membership, so the version that members use does not include the new function.
Every time a team updates the working draft of an agent, it must prepare the agent so that the agent includes the latest changes. A missing Prepare step would explain a function that never runs. Here, "Please pause my membership" reaches pause_membership, so the agent that members use already has the new function.

INCORRECT: The temperature of the orchestration step is too high, so the model picks one of the two membership functions at random for each request.
Temperature is one of the inference parameters that the trace shows for each step. A high temperature makes the output of a model vary more from one request to the next. Here, the same message leads to cancel_membership every time, so the choice does not change between requests, and a random pick does not explain the result.

questions.promptHtml:
An airline runs a question-answering assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Most customers type on their phones, so many questions arrive with typos, in lowercase or with extra spaces. The team must choose one of two models, and it has a dataset of 400 real questions with a reference answer for each.
For each model, the team wants a score that shows how much the answers change when the same questions contain small errors like these. The score must come from a managed evaluation job, with no human reviewers.
Which evaluation should the team run?
questions.promptText:
An airline runs a question-answering assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Most customers type on their phones, so many questions arrive with typos, in lowercase or with extra spaces. The team must choose one of two models, and it has a dataset of 400 real questions with a reference answer for each.
For each model, the team wants a score that shows how much the answers change when the same questions contain small errors like these. The score must come from a managed evaluation job, with no human reviewers.
Which evaluation should the team run?

options.text: Create a model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model that uses a judge model to score the answers to the team's dataset for correctness and completeness.
Create an automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model with the question and answer task type, the accuracy metric and the team's dataset.
Create a human-based model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock that asks a group of employees to rate the answers of both models to the team's dataset.
Create an automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model with the question and answer task type, the robustness metric and the team's dataset.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model with the question and answer task type, the robustness metric and the team's dataset.
The robustness metric of an automatic model evaluation measures how much the output of a model changes after small changes to the input that keep its meaning. Amazon Bedrock makes these changes itself. It converts the text to lowercase, adds keyboard typos, adds or removes spaces and makes other small changes to each prompt in the dataset.

For the question and answer task, the score compares the F1 score of the answers to the changed prompts with the F1 score of the answers to the original prompts. A lower score means that the answers change less. This is the score that the team wants, and the job needs no reviewers.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.1: "Develop comprehensive assessment frameworks to evaluate the quality and effectiveness of FM outputs beyond traditional ML evaluation approaches"

Sources:

  • Review metrics for an automated model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock (console)
  • Model evaluation task types in Amazon Bedrock
  • Use metrics to understand model performance

INCORRECT: Create a model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model that uses a judge model to score the answers to the team's dataset for correctness and completeness.
A judge model can score each answer for correctness and completeness, and it uses the reference answer when the dataset has one. These metrics rate each answer on its own. They do not compare the answers to a question with and without small errors.

INCORRECT: Create an automatic model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock for each model with the question and answer task type, the accuracy metric and the team's dataset.
The accuracy metric for the question and answer task compares each answer with the reference answer and gives an F1 score. It shows how correct each model is on the questions as they are. It does not change the questions, so it cannot show how much the answers change when the questions contain typos or extra spaces.

INCORRECT: Create a human-based model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock that asks a group of employees to rate the answers of both models to the team's dataset.
In a human-based evaluation, people rate the answers. The team wants the score from a managed job with no human reviewers, so this option does not meet the requirement. The employees would also rate answers to the questions as they are, not to changed questions.

questions.promptHtml:
A real estate company writes its property listing texts with a model that another vendor offers only through its own API, outside AWS. The vendor does not share the model weights. The team wants to know if a Claude Sonnet model in Amazon Bedrock writes better listings.
Both models must be scored on the same 300 prompts, by the same judge model and with the same metrics. The team has no reviewers for this work.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A real estate company writes its property listing texts with a model that another vendor offers only through its own API, outside AWS. The vendor does not share the model weights. The team wants to know if a Claude Sonnet model in Amazon Bedrock writes better listings.
Both models must be scored on the same 300 prompts, by the same judge model and with the same metrics. The team has no reviewers for this work.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Import the vendor's model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, and run a model evaluation job with a judge model for each of the two models.

Add the vendor model's answers to a prompt dataset as saved inference responses, and run a model evaluation job with a judge model on it. Run a second job for Claude Sonnet with the same judge model and metrics.
Create a human-based model evaluation job that shows the answers of both models to a work team, and compare the ratings that the team gives each model.

Write an AWS Lambda function that sends each answer of both models with a scoring prompt to the judge model in Amazon Bedrock. Store the scores in Amazon DynamoDB, and compare the average score of each model across all 300 prompts.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Add the vendor model's answers to a prompt dataset as saved inference responses, and run a model evaluation job with a judge model on it. Run a second job for Claude Sonnet with the same judge model and metrics.
A model evaluation job with a judge model can score a model that runs outside Amazon Bedrock. The team puts the vendor model's saved answers in the prompt dataset, and Amazon Bedrock skips the model call and scores the answers that it gets. A job with saved answers accepts only one model identifier, so Claude Sonnet gets its own job. Both jobs use the same prompts, judge model and metrics, so the two scores can be compared, and the team writes no scoring code.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.2: "Create systematic model evaluation systems to identify optimal configurations"
Example: "Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations"

Sources:

  • Evaluate model performance using another LLM as a judge
  • Create a prompt dataset for a model evaluation job that uses a model as judge
  • Use Custom model import to import a customized open-source model into Amazon Bedrock

INCORRECT: Import the vendor's model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, and run a model evaluation job with a judge model for each of the two models.
Custom Model Import creates a model in Amazon Bedrock from model files in Amazon S3, such as the weights in the safetensors format. The vendor does not share the weights, so the team has nothing to import.

INCORRECT: Create a human-based model evaluation job that shows the answers of both models to a work team, and compare the ratings that the team gives each model.
In a human-based evaluation, people rate the answers. The team has no reviewers, and the requirement asks for one judge model, not human ratings.

INCORRECT: Write an AWS Lambda function that sends each answer of both models with a scoring prompt to the judge model in Amazon Bedrock. Store the scores in Amazon DynamoDB, and compare the average score of each model across all 300 prompts.
A Lambda function can send each answer to a judge model and store the scores. This works, but the team must write the scoring prompts, run the calls, handle errors and build the report. The managed evaluation job already does this work, so this option has more operational overhead.

questions.promptHtml:
An online learning platform has a study assistant in its app. An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Students rate each answer from 1 to 5 stars, and the app stores each rating with the user ID and the time.
This week, the team published a new prompt version on Monday and moved half of the users to a new model on Wednesday. The average rating dropped, and the team cannot tell which change caused it. The team must track real user ratings for each prompt version and model.
Which combination of steps will show the ratings for each prompt version and model?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
An online learning platform has a study assistant in its app. An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Students rate each answer from 1 to 5 stars, and the app stores each rating with the user ID and the time.
This week, the team published a new prompt version on Monday and moved half of the users to a new model on Wednesday. The average rating dropped, and the team cannot tell which change caused it. The team must track real user ratings for each prompt version and model.
Which combination of steps will show the ratings for each prompt version and model?
Select TWO.

options.text: Keep each rating with the user ID and the time, and match each rating time to the time when each prompt version was published.
Have the Lambda function return a response ID with each answer, and save the prompt version and the model ID for each response ID in Amazon DynamoDB.
Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to find the answers that users rated low.
Run a model evaluation job with a judge model on a fixed prompt dataset each time that the team publishes a prompt version or moves users to a new model.
Have the app send the response ID with each rating, and publish each rating as a CloudWatch custom metric with the prompt version and the model ID as dimensions.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Have the Lambda function return a response ID with each answer, and save the prompt version and the model ID for each response ID in Amazon DynamoDB.
A rating helps only when the team knows what produced the rated answer. Prompt Management gives each prompt version a number, and the function knows which version and which model it used for each answer. With a response ID for each answer, the function can save that pair. This record links every answer to the prompt version and the model that wrote it.

CORRECT: Have the app send the response ID with each rating, and publish each rating as a CloudWatch custom metric with the prompt version and the model ID as dimensions.
The app sends the same response ID with the rating, so each rating can be matched to its prompt version and model. A CloudWatch custom metric can carry dimensions, which are name and value pairs. With the prompt version and the model ID as dimensions, the team can chart the ratings for each version and model and set alarms on them. A drop then shows up in the ratings of the prompt version or the model that the team changed.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.3: "Develop user-centered evaluation mechanisms to continuously improve FM performance based on user experience"
Example: "rating systems for model outputs"

Sources:

  • Create a version of a prompt in Prompt management
  • Publish custom metrics (PutMetricData / EMF)
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3

INCORRECT: Keep each rating with the user ID and the time, and match each rating time to the time when each prompt version was published.
Matching times can work when only one thing changes at a time. Here the two changes overlap: from Wednesday, half of the users get the new model while the new prompt version is live. A rating time cannot show which model a user got, so this option cannot separate the two changes.

INCORRECT: Turn on model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock, and use CloudWatch Logs Insights to find the answers that users rated low.
Model invocation logging records the request, the response, the model ID and other metadata of each model call. It does not record the ratings, which the app keeps with only a user ID and a time. Nothing links a rating to a logged call, so the team cannot find the answers that users rated low.

INCORRECT: Run a model evaluation job with a judge model on a fixed prompt dataset each time that the team publishes a prompt version or moves users to a new model.
A judge model scores the answers to test prompts. This is a useful check before a change, but it does not use the ratings of real users, and the team must track those ratings.

questions.promptHtml:
A company sells event tickets online. An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock to write each event description, and a parser reads each reply in a fixed JSON layout. The team keeps a regression test set of 200 saved inputs with layout checks.
The Amazon Bedrock console now shows the model version as Legacy, with an end-of-life date in four months. A newer version of the same model is Active. No reply in production may break the parser, and descriptions must continue after the end-of-life date.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A company sells event tickets online. An AWS Lambda function calls a model in Amazon Bedrock to write each event description, and a parser reads each reply in a fixed JSON layout. The team keeps a regression test set of 200 saved inputs with layout checks.
The Amazon Bedrock console now shows the model version as Legacy, with an end-of-life date in four months. A newer version of the same model is Active. No reply in production may break the parser, and descriptions must continue after the end-of-life date.
Which combination of steps will meet these requirements?
Select TWO.

options.text: Run the regression test set against the Active version, and change the prompt until every reply passes the layout checks.
Keep the current model ID, because Amazon Bedrock moves the calls to the Active version on the end-of-life date.
Change the model ID to the Active version today, and run the regression test set once a week after the switch.
When all tests pass, change the model ID in the Lambda function configuration to the fixed ID of the Active version.
Move the calls to a cross-Region inference profile for the Legacy version, so other Regions keep serving it after the end-of-life date.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Run the regression test set against the Active version, and change the prompt until every reply passes the layout checks.
A regression test set holds saved inputs and the checks that each output must pass. A newer model version can answer the same prompt in another way, so the team runs the set against the Active version first. If a reply breaks the layout, the team changes the prompt and runs the set again. The team finds a broken layout before any reply reaches the parser in production.

CORRECT: When all tests pass, change the model ID in the Lambda function configuration to the fixed ID of the Active version.
The function calls one fixed model ID, so the model version changes only when the team changes that ID. After the tests pass, the team changes the ID to the Active version. Requests to the Legacy version fail after the end-of-life date, so this switch must happen before that date.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.4: "Create systematic quality assurance processes to maintain consistent performance standards for FMs"
Example: "regression testing for model outputs"

Sources:

  • Model lifecycle
  • Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference

INCORRECT: Keep the current model ID, because Amazon Bedrock moves the calls to the Active version on the end-of-life date.
Amazon Bedrock does not move calls to a newer version. After the end-of-life date, requests to the old version fail, and the migration does not happen automatically. With this option, the descriptions stop on that date.

INCORRECT: Change the model ID to the Active version today, and run the regression test set once a week after the switch.
This option switches first and tests later. The new version may reply in another layout, and a weekly test would find the problem only after replies had already reached the parser. The question says that no reply in production may break the parser.

INCORRECT: Move the calls to a cross-Region inference profile for the Legacy version, so other Regions keep serving it after the end-of-life date.
Cross-Region inference sends requests to compute in other AWS Regions. It does not extend the life of a model version: after the end-of-life date, Amazon Bedrock removes the model from all AWS Regions, so no Region can serve it.

questions.promptHtml:
A telecom company runs a plan-change agent for its customers. The agent is built with LangGraph, and it runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with AgentCore Observability turned on. Its tools look up the current plan, compare plans and change the plan.
Some customers say that the agent compared plans when they asked for a change, and that their request was never finished. The team wants scores from a sample of live sessions for two things: whether each session completed the customer's request, and whether the agent chose the right tool at each step.
Which combination of steps will give the team these two scores?
Select TWO.
questions.promptText:
A telecom company runs a plan-change agent for its customers. The agent is built with LangGraph, and it runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with AgentCore Observability turned on. Its tools look up the current plan, compare plans and change the plan.
Some customers say that the agent compared plans when they asked for a change, and that their request was never finished. The team wants scores from a sample of live sessions for two things: whether each session completed the customer's request, and whether the agent chose the right tool at each step.
Which combination of steps will give the team these two scores?
Select TWO.

options.text: Run a model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock each day with a judge model that scores the final replies of the agent for correctness.
Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query each day that counts the tool calls in each session, and set an alarm for when the count rises.
Create an online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations for the agent, and add the built-in Goal success rate evaluator.
Add the built-in Tool selection accuracy evaluator to the same online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations.
Add the built-in Tool parameter accuracy evaluator to the same online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Create an online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations for the agent, and add the built-in Goal success rate evaluator.
AgentCore Evaluations scores agents from their traces, and it supports agents built with LangGraph. An online evaluation configuration evaluates live traffic as the traces arrive, and its sampling setting chooses the share of sessions to score. The built-in Goal success rate evaluator works at the session level. It checks whether the agent completed all user goals in the conversation, so it shows whether each request was finished.

CORRECT: Add the built-in Tool selection accuracy evaluator to the same online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations.
The built-in Tool selection accuracy evaluator works at the tool level. It checks whether the agent chose the right tool for the situation, for example the change tool when the customer asked for a change. One configuration can hold up to 25 evaluators, so both scores come from the same sample of sessions.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.7: "Develop agent performance frameworks to ensure that agents perform tasks correctly and efficiently"
Example: "task completion rate measurements"

Sources:

  • Evaluate agent performance with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
  • Create online evaluation
  • Prompt templates

INCORRECT: Run a model evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock each day with a judge model that scores the final replies of the agent for correctness.
A judge model that reads only the final replies sees what the agent said, not which tools it called. It cannot score each tool choice, and a reply can sound correct even when the plan was never changed.

INCORRECT: Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query each day that counts the tool calls in each session, and set an alarm for when the count rises.
A count of tool calls shows how busy each session was. A session with few calls can still use the wrong tool, so the count shows neither the right tool choice nor a finished request.

INCORRECT: Add the built-in Tool parameter accuracy evaluator to the same online evaluation configuration in AgentCore Evaluations.
Tool parameter accuracy also works at the tool level, but it checks whether the agent used the right information in the inputs of each tool call. The customers' problem is a wrong tool: the compare tool in place of the change tool. This evaluator does not score the choice of tool.
