A university runs a student services assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. To test two chunking strategies, the team built two knowledge bases from the same documents. It ran a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job on each one, with the same prompt dataset, judge model and metrics.
The heads of student services must choose one knowledge base in a meeting tomorrow. They want to see the scores of both jobs for each metric in one view, with the difference between the scores.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A university runs a student services assistant on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. To test two chunking strategies, the team built two knowledge bases from the same documents. It ran a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job on each one, with the same prompt dataset, judge model and metrics.
The heads of student services must choose one knowledge base in a meeting tomorrow. They want to see the scores of both jobs for each metric in one view, with the difference between the scores.
Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Download the result files of both jobs from Amazon S3, and build an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard that shows the scores of each metric side by side.
Open the report card of each evaluation job in the Amazon Bedrock console, and show the two report cards in the meeting one after the other.
In the Amazon Bedrock console, select both knowledge base evaluation jobs, and choose Compare to show the scores and the difference for each metric.
Run one new knowledge base evaluation job that includes both knowledge bases, and show the report card of that new job in the meeting.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: In the Amazon Bedrock console, select both knowledge base evaluation jobs, and choose Compare to show the scores and the difference for each metric.
The Amazon Bedrock console can compare the results of evaluation jobs when the jobs cover the same metrics, as these two jobs do. The At a glance tab shows the metrics of both jobs in a spider chart. The Evaluation details tab shows the results for each metric, with the difference in scores. The team builds nothing, so this option has the least operational overhead.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.1.8: "Create comprehensive reporting systems to communicate performance metrics and insights effectively to stakeholders for FM implementations"
Example: "visualization tools"

Sources:

  • New RAG evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge capabilities in Amazon Bedrock
  • Review RAG evaluation job reports and metrics
  • EvaluationInferenceConfig

INCORRECT: Download the result files of both jobs from Amazon S3, and build an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard that shows the scores of each metric side by side.
The results of each job are also stored in the Amazon S3 bucket that the team chose for the job, so a Quick Sight dashboard can show them. But the team must read the result files, prepare the data and build the charts before tomorrow. This works, and it adds work that the console already does.

INCORRECT: Open the report card of each evaluation job in the Amazon Bedrock console, and show the two report cards in the meeting one after the other.
Each report card shows the results of one job. Shown one after the other, the two cards give no single view of both jobs and no difference for each metric, which the heads of student services asked for.

INCORRECT: Run one new knowledge base evaluation job that includes both knowledge bases, and show the report card of that new job in the meeting.
A knowledge base evaluation job takes the configuration of exactly one knowledge base, so one job cannot include both. The team would also run the evaluation again, although it already has the results of both jobs.

questions.promptHtml:
A bank's mobile app sorts each card transaction into one of six spending categories, such as Groceries, Dining and Fuel. Amazon Nova Lite in Amazon Bedrock picks the category, with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management.
Last week, the team released a new prompt version with 12 example transactions and their categories. The model and its inference settings did not change. Since the release, the share of transactions in Dining has grown from about 10 percent to about 35 percent. Many of them are grocery and fuel payments from merchants that the earlier version sorted correctly. When the team moved a Groceries example to the end of the list, nothing changed.
What is the cause of this issue?
questions.promptText:
A bank's mobile app sorts each card transaction into one of six spending categories, such as Groceries, Dining and Fuel. Amazon Nova Lite in Amazon Bedrock picks the category, with a prompt from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management.
Last week, the team released a new prompt version with 12 example transactions and their categories. The model and its inference settings did not change. Since the release, the share of transactions in Dining has grown from about 10 percent to about 35 percent. Many of them are grocery and fuel payments from merchants that the earlier version sorted correctly. When the team moved a Groceries example to the end of the list, nothing changed.
What is the cause of this issue?

options.text: The temperature in the inference settings is too high, so the model chooses a category at random.
The last example in the prompt shows the Dining category, and the model repeats the last category that it sees.
Amazon Nova Lite does not know many of the merchant names that appear in the card transactions.
Most of the 12 example transactions in the new prompt version show the Dining category.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Most of the 12 example transactions in the new prompt version show the Dining category.
Examples in a prompt show the model what a correct answer looks like, and the model follows them. The Amazon Nova prompting guide says that the examples should represent the distribution of the inputs and outputs that you expect, because bias in the examples can make the outputs biased too.

Here, the problem started with the new prompt version, which adds the 12 examples, while the model and its settings stayed the same. The extra answers do not spread across the categories. They all go to one category, Dining, even for grocery and fuel payments that the model sorted correctly before. That pattern fits a set of examples that shows mostly Dining. The team should use examples that cover all six categories in a mix close to the real transactions.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.3: "Troubleshoot prompt engineering problems to improve FM response quality and consistency beyond basic prompt adjustments"
Example: "version comparison"

Sources:

  • Provide examples (few-shot prompting)
  • Deploy a prompt to your application using versions in Prompt management
  • Influence response generation with inference parameters

INCORRECT: The temperature in the inference settings is too high, so the model chooses a category at random.
Temperature controls how random the output is. A higher value makes the model more likely to choose less likely outputs, so the answers vary more. This option does not fit for two reasons. The inference settings did not change, and the earlier prompt version gave good results with the same settings. Also, random choices would spread the wrong answers across many categories, but here the extra answers go to one category, Dining.

INCORRECT: The last example in the prompt shows the Dining category, and the model repeats the last category that it sees.
This option says that the position of one example decides the answer. The team already tested the order. When it moved a Groceries example to the end of the list, the results did not change. So the position of the examples is not the cause.

INCORRECT: Amazon Nova Lite does not know many of the merchant names that appear in the card transactions.
If the model did not know the merchant names, the earlier prompt version would also have sorted these payments wrong, because it used the same model. The question states that the earlier version sorted the same grocery and fuel merchants correctly. So the merchant names are not the cause. The change came with the new prompt version.

questions.promptHtml:
A grocery delivery company writes each product description with a prompt template in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Over six months, several team members edited the template, and the inference settings did not change. Before these edits, the descriptions listed every allergen each time.
Now, for products with many allergens, some descriptions list every allergen and some list only a few. A template test that sends one such product 10 times gets both results. Products with few allergens always get the same description. The model invocation logs in CloudWatch Logs show the same prompt text in every request, with all allergens in the data.
What is the MOST likely cause of these inconsistent descriptions?
questions.promptText:
A grocery delivery company writes each product description with a prompt template in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Over six months, several team members edited the template, and the inference settings did not change. Before these edits, the descriptions listed every allergen each time.
Now, for products with many allergens, some descriptions list every allergen and some list only a few. A template test that sends one such product 10 times gets both results. Products with few allergens always get the same description. The model invocation logs in CloudWatch Logs show the same prompt text in every request, with all allergens in the data.
What is the MOST likely cause of these inconsistent descriptions?

options.text: Some application servers still call an older version of the prompt, which has no rule that asks the model to list all allergens of a product.
Two rules from different edits conflict for products with many allergens, so the model follows one rule in some runs and the other in other runs.
The temperature is too high for this task, so the model writes a different description each time that it gets the same product.
The product data of some products leaves out allergens, so the model cannot list every allergen for those products.

questions.explanationHtml:
CORRECT: Two rules from different edits conflict for products with many allergens, so the model follows one rule in some runs and the other in other runs.
When many people edit a template over time, a new rule can conflict with an older one. For example, one rule asks the model to list every allergen, and a later rule asks for a short description. A product with few allergens meets both rules, so its description stays the same.

A product with many allergens cannot meet both, so the model follows one rule in some runs and the other rule in other runs. The template test shows this pattern on one input, and the logs show that the prompt text is the same in every request. The fix is to read the rules together and remove the conflict.

Exam Guide Reference:
Skill 5.2.5: "Troubleshoot prompt maintenance issues to continuously improve the performance of FM interactions"
Example: "template testing and CloudWatch Logs to diagnose prompt confusion"

Sources:

  • Create a version of a prompt in Prompt management
  • Monitor model invocation using CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3
  • Influence response generation with inference parameters

INCORRECT: Some application servers still call an older version of the prompt, which has no rule that asks the model to list all allergens of a product.
Each prompt version is a snapshot of the template, so an older version could give other results. But the logs show the same prompt text in every request, so every request uses the same version.

INCORRECT: The temperature is too high for this task, so the model writes a different description each time that it gets the same product.
A higher temperature makes the responses more random. But the inference settings did not change, and before the edits the descriptions listed every allergen each time. The variation started with the edits to the template, not with the temperature.

INCORRECT: The product data of some products leaves out allergens, so the model cannot list every allergen for those products.
Missing allergens in the product data would explain a short list. But the logs show all allergens in the product data, and the same product gives both results in the template test.
